name: Classic-Style Test 1
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: City planner: Some residents argue that Harlow’s downtown parking garage should be demolished because it is rarely more than half full. But the garage’s low usage reflects its high hourly rates, which the council set before the new transit line reduced downtown traffic. Lowering those rates would probably fill the garage. So the garage should be kept, at least until lower rates have been tried.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the city planner’s argument?
choices: Residents who want the garage demolished have misjudged how heavily drivers actually use it, even during the busiest hours of the day.
The garage is rarely more than half full mainly because the council set its hourly rates too high.
Lowering the garage’s hourly rates would probably bring in enough additional drivers to fill the garage.
The council set the garage’s current rates before the new transit line reduced the amount of downtown traffic.
The downtown garage should not be demolished at least until lower hourly rates have been tried there.
questions.explanation: The planner’s point, signaled by “So,” is that the garage should be kept until lower rates are tried, which (E) restates. (C) is the tempting choice, but the prediction about lower rates is offered as a reason for keeping the garage; (B) is likewise a supporting premise. (A) misreads the planner, who accepts that usage is low and disputes only its cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The garage should be kept, at least until lower rates have been tried.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Low usage is caused by high rates, set before the transit line cut traffic; lowering the rates would probably fill the garage.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. This is a rebuttal: the residents say tear it down because it's half empty. The planner says the emptiness comes from the prices, cheaper prices would fill it, so keep it until we try that. The word "So" flags the conclusion. Think of a restaurant owner saying: "The new dish isn't selling because it's overpriced, a lower price would sell it, so don't pull it off the menu yet." The point is "don't pull it yet," not the pricing story.

choices.note: The planner never says the residents misjudged usage. The planner accepts that the garage is rarely more than half full and only disputes what that fact means. Wrong claim attributed to the speaker.
This is a premise. The planner uses the high-rates explanation to undercut the residents' reason. It supports the conclusion; it isn't the conclusion.

Tempting. It's the planner's boldest claim, so it feels like the point. But ask why the planner says it: to show the garage is worth keeping. A prediction offered as a reason is a premise. The conclusion is the claim the others are trying to prove, not the most interesting one.
Background detail. It explains why the rates are now too high. It sits at the bottom of the support structure.

CORRECT. "Kept, at least until lower rates have been tried" means the same thing as "not demolished at least until lower rates have been tried." It's what the "So" introduces and what every other sentence is there to support.

questions.stimulus:
Ana: The old mill on Fenwick Creek should be restored and opened as a museum. It is the town’s last link to the industry on which the town was founded, and visitors would see how our community grew.

Ben: The mill is certainly historically important. But restoring it would cost far more than the town could ever raise. The town should instead put up a plaque and a small exhibit at the library, which would preserve the mill’s story cheaply.
questions.stem: Ana and Ben disagree over whether
choices: the mill is the town’s last remaining link to the industry on which the town was founded
restoring the mill would cost more money than the town could realistically ever raise
the history associated with the mill is worth preserving in some form
the town should restore the mill and then open it to the public as a museum
visitors would learn more from a museum in the mill than from an exhibit at the library
questions.explanation: Ana says the mill should be restored as a museum; Ben says restoration costs too much and the town should do something cheaper instead, so they disagree over (D). (C) is the trap: both value the mill’s history, so they agree on it. (A) is Ana’s claim alone, (B) is Ben’s alone, and neither speaker compares what visitors would learn, as (E) requires.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ana: Restore the mill as a museum; it's the town's last link to its founding industry.; Ben: It's historically important, but restoring it costs far too much; put up a plaque and a library exhibit instead.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Ana says: restore it, make it a museum. Ben says: too expensive, do this cheaper thing instead. That "instead" is Ben's no. Notice what they share: both think the mill's story matters. Ben even calls it "certainly historically important." So history is common ground, and the fight is over the museum.

choices.note: Ana's claim only. Ben never says whether the mill is the town's last link to its founding industry; he says only that it is historically important. One speaker silent means no disagreement.
Ben's claim only. Ana never addresses cost, so we can't say she rejects it.

Tempting, because the dialogue is all about history. But this is what they agree on: Ana wants the history shown, and Ben wants to "preserve the mill's story." Agreement is not a point of disagreement.
CORRECT. Ana says the mill should be restored and opened as a museum. Ben says restoration costs more than the town could raise and the town should "instead" do a plaque and exhibit. Yes versus no.
Neither speaker compares what visitors would learn from a museum versus an exhibit. Ana mentions visitors, but she doesn't rank the two options. Unsupported for both.

questions.stimulus: An observatory recently replaced its aging telescope with a new one whose much larger mirror gathers far more light, making faint galaxies considerably easier to detect. Yet in its first year of use, the new telescope detected fewer faint galaxies than the old telescope had detected in its final year, even though astronomers aimed both instruments at the same regions of the sky.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Telescopes with larger mirrors are more expensive to maintain.
The observatory’s astronomers had expected the new telescope to detect many more faint galaxies than the old one detected.
Faint galaxies are considerably harder for any telescope to detect than bright galaxies at a comparable distance are.
In its first year, the new telescope was often shut down for calibration and so observed far fewer hours.
The old telescope had been in continuous use at the observatory for several decades before it was finally replaced, and its retirement was marked by a public ceremony.
questions.explanation: A better instrument can still produce a smaller total if it is used much less, and (D) says the new telescope spent far less time observing, which resolves the puzzle. (B) merely restates the expectation that makes the result surprising, and (C) is true of both telescopes alike, so it cannot explain a difference between them.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The new telescope gathers far more light and makes faint galaxies easier to detect, but in its first year it detected fewer faint galaxies than the old one did in its last year.

breakdown.analysis: How can a better tool produce a smaller total? Totals depend on two things: how good the tool is and how much it gets used. The stimulus rules out "it looked at different sky," so look for something that made the new telescope get used less. It's like buying a faster car and still logging fewer miles this year because it sat in the shop for months. Prephrase: the new telescope wasn't observing as much.

choices.note: Cost has nothing to do with how many galaxies it detects once it's built. Irrelevant.
This just restates why the result is surprising. Expectations don't explain why the expectations weren't met.
True of both telescopes equally. A fact that applies to both sides can't explain a difference between them. In a paradox about a comparison, you need a factor that differs between the two things.

CORRECT. Fewer hours of observing means fewer chances to detect anything. Even a far better telescope can rack up a smaller total if it's shut down for calibration much of the year. Both facts in the paradox can now be true.
So the old telescope was old. That makes it even stranger that it beat the new one. Doesn't resolve anything.

questions.stimulus: In a recent survey of dog owners, those who walk their dogs on retractable leashes reported far more incidents of their dogs lunging at passersby than did those who use fixed-length leashes. The two groups of owners walked their dogs for about the same amount of time each day. Evidently, the extra slack that retractable leashes provide encourages dogs to lunge.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on reports from dog owners rather than on observations made by professional trainers or other neutral experts
presumes, without providing justification, that any dog that lunges at passersby must have been poorly trained by its owner
overlooks the possibility that owners of dogs prone to lunging are more likely to choose retractable leashes
takes for granted that every dog walked on a retractable leash will at some point lunge at passersby
treats an undesirable behavior as though it were therefore a common one
questions.explanation: The argument infers that the leash causes the lunging from a mere correlation, ignoring that the dogs themselves may differ: owners of lunge-prone dogs might favor retractable leashes, which is (C). (A) is tempting because self-reports can be unreliable, but nothing turns on owners being worse judges than trainers of whether their dogs lunge. (D) attributes a claim about every dog that the argument never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The extra slack of retractable leashes encourages dogs to lunge.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Owners using retractable leashes reported far more lunging incidents than owners using fixed-length leashes; both groups walked their dogs about equally long.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the two go together? Correlation isn't causation. The argument even rules out one rival (more walking time), but not the biggest one: the dogs may be different to begin with. Maybe owners of wild, pully dogs pick retractable leashes because those dogs hate short leads. It's like saying hospitals make people sick because people in hospitals are sicker than people outside. Prephrase: the argument ignores that the dogs on retractable leashes may already be more lunge-prone.

choices.note: Tempting, because self-reports can be shaky. But owners are perfectly able to notice their dog lunging, and nothing in the argument depends on owners being worse judges than trainers. This names a source problem the argument doesn't really have.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our customers say our coffee is the best in town, so it must be better than any coffee a professional taster has rated.

choices.note: Training never comes up. The argument blames the leash, not poor training, so this describes an assumption the argument doesn't make.
choices.example: Example of flaw: That dog jumped on a guest, so its owner obviously never trained it.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the alternative explanation: the dogs differ before the leash ever enters the picture. If lunge-prone dogs end up on retractable leashes, leash type would correlate with lunging even if slack had zero effect.
Too strong. The argument talks about more incidents in one group, not that every retractable-leash dog lunges. It doesn't need or assume an "every" claim.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Retractable leashes encourage lunging, so my neighbor's dog, which is on one, must lunge at people.

choices.note: The argument never argues from lunging being undesirable, and it's not trying to prove lunging is common. It's a causal claim about leashes. Describes a different flaw entirely.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Littering is terrible, so it must be happening all over this park.

questions.stimulus: Last spring a bistro began printing calorie counts beside each item on its menu. Since then, sales of the bistro’s two highest-calorie desserts have fallen by nearly a third, while sales of its fruit plates have risen by about the same number of orders. The bistro’s owner concludes that the calorie counts led many diners to choose lighter desserts.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the owner’s argument?
choices: Several regular diners have told the owner that they appreciate being able to see calorie counts on the menu.
Over the same period, dessert sales at nearby restaurants that do not print calorie counts showed no comparable shift.
The bistro’s two highest-calorie desserts are also the most expensive desserts that the bistro offers on its menu.
Many of the bistro’s diners say they rarely read the menu closely.
Last spring the bistro also hired a new pastry chef, who redesigned the fruit plates and their presentation.
questions.explanation: The owner attributes a sales shift to the calorie counts, so the argument is helped by evidence that the shift did not happen where there were no calorie counts, as (B) shows; that makes a general change in tastes a less likely cause. (A) is tempting but shows only that diners like the counts, not that the counts changed what they ordered. (E) offers a rival explanation and (D) suggests diners ignored the counts, so both weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The calorie counts led many diners to choose lighter desserts.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the menu started showing calorie counts, sales of the two highest-calorie desserts fell almost a third and fruit plate sales rose.

breakdown.analysis: Before-and-after causal argument. Calorie counts went up, then heavy dessert sales went down, so the counts did it. But did anything else change? A citywide diet trend or the season could do the same thing. To strengthen, rule out those rivals. The cleanest way is a control group: places without calorie counts that didn't see the shift. It's like testing a new fertilizer: your tomatoes grew bigger, but did your neighbor's unfertilized tomatoes grow bigger too?

choices.note: Tempting, but liking the counts isn't the same as changing what you order. A diner can appreciate the information and still order the chocolate cake. Doesn't connect counts to choices.

CORRECT. This is the control group. Nearby restaurants without calorie counts saw no similar shift, so a general change in tastes or the weather is less likely to be the cause. That leaves the calorie counts looking more like the reason.
If anything this hurts. If the heavy desserts are also the priciest, maybe people cut back because of price. It opens a rival cause rather than supporting the calorie explanation.
This weakens. If diners barely read the menu, it's hard for numbers printed on the menu to be driving their choices.

Weakens. A new pastry chef who redesigned the fruit plates is a rival explanation for why fruit plates got more popular, at exactly the same time. An answer that adds a second change during the same period almost always hurts a before-and-after argument.

questions.stimulus: Principal: This year our school stopped assigning weekend homework, chiefly in order to reduce student stress. Yet students’ average score on the annual stress survey, which every student completes each spring, is no lower this year than it was last year. So, whatever its other merits, eliminating weekend homework has not reduced student stress.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the principal’s argument?
choices: Students who no longer have weekend homework now spend more of their weekend time on extracurricular activities, such as sports, music lessons, and volunteer work.
Reducing the amount of homework is the single most effective way for a school to reduce student stress.
Students’ average stress-survey score rose this year.
Most students had regularly been completing all of their weekend homework before the new policy took effect.
No other change this year raised students’ stress enough to offset a reduction due to the policy.
questions.explanation: Unchanged survey scores show the policy failed only if nothing else pushed stress up at the same time; if some other change raised stress by as much as the policy lowered it, the flat scores would hide a real effect. That is (E). (B) is tempting but goes much further than needed, and (C) is not required, since unchanged scores are enough for the argument. Negating (D) actually helps the principal.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eliminating weekend homework has not reduced student stress.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The policy started this year; average stress survey scores are no lower than last year.

breakdown.analysis: Do flat scores really mean the policy did nothing? Not if two forces cancel out: the policy lowers stress while something else raises it. Picture a diet that works, but you also stopped exercising, and the scale doesn't move. The diet still worked. We need an answer that says nothing else was pushing stress up enough to mask the drop. Use the negation test: if negating a choice wrecks the argument, it's required.

choices.note: Negate it and nothing happens. Whether students moved to extracurriculars or not, the argument is about the stress scores. Irrelevant.
choices.negation: Students who no longer have weekend homework do not spend more of their weekend time on extracurricular activities.

choices.note: Too strong. The principal only claims this policy didn't work, not anything about which method is best. Negate it (homework cuts aren't the best method) and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Reducing the amount of homework is not the single most effective way for a school to reduce student stress.

choices.note: Not required. "No lower" already does the job. Negated, scores didn't rise (say, they stayed exactly the same), and the argument works just fine.
choices.negation: Students’ average stress-survey score did not rise this year.

choices.note: Tempting, since if kids weren't doing the homework anyway, cutting it couldn't help. But that would actually support the principal's conclusion. Negating it doesn't hurt the argument; it gives another reason the policy might not have worked.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most students had regularly been completing all of their weekend homework before the new policy took effect.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, some other change did raise stress enough to offset a real reduction. Then flat scores tell you nothing about the policy, and the conclusion falls apart. Negation destroys the argument, so it's required.
choices.negation: Some other change this year raised students' stress enough to offset a reduction due to the policy.

questions.stimulus: Last year, customers who bought the Lumo vacuum with the extended warranty brought it in for repairs far less often than customers who bought it without the warranty. The warranty includes a free yearly tune-up that other customers do not receive. Lumo’s marketing director concludes that the tune-up must be reducing the number of breakdowns these vacuums suffer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the marketing director’s argument?
choices: Most customers who bought the extended warranty brought their vacuums in for the free yearly tune-up last year.
Customers who did not buy the extended warranty must pay the full cost of any repair their vacuum needs.
Lumo vacuums break down less often than most competing models.
During each yearly tune-up, technicians fix any malfunction they find, and such fixes are not recorded as repairs.
Customers who bought the extended warranty used their vacuums no more often, on average, than customers who did not buy it.
questions.explanation: The director treats fewer recorded repair visits as evidence of fewer breakdowns. (D) shows the comparison is skewed: warranty holders’ malfunctions are often fixed during tune-ups and never counted as repairs, so their lower repair count need not mean fewer breakdowns. (A) strengthens the argument by confirming that warranty holders actually got the tune-ups, and (E) strengthens it by ruling out lighter use as the explanation. (B), if anything, strengthens it too: customers who must pay for repairs would tend to bring vacuums in less often, yet they still had more repair visits.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The free yearly tune-up must be reducing breakdowns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Warranty customers brought their vacuums in for repairs less often than non-warranty customers; only warranty customers get the yearly tune-up.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of repair visits really the same as the number of breakdowns? Notice the switch: the evidence is about repair visits, but the conclusion is about breakdowns. If breakdowns get fixed some other way, repair visits can drop even when breakdowns don't. It's like saying a gym's members get sick less because they file fewer sick-day forms, when the gym's clinic quietly treats them on site. We need an answer that says warranty holders' breakdowns are being handled without counting as repair visits.

choices.note: This strengthens. It confirms warranty customers actually got the tune-ups, which the argument needs.

Tempting, because it points to a difference between the groups. But it pushes the wrong way: non-warranty customers have to pay, which should make them come in less, yet they still came in more. That makes their higher repair rate look like real breakdowns.
Comparing Lumo to competitors doesn't touch the comparison between warranty and non-warranty Lumo owners. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. Malfunctions get fixed during the tune-up and aren't recorded as repairs. So warranty holders could break down just as often; their breakdowns just show up as tune-ups. The lower repair count no longer shows fewer breakdowns.

Tempting if you’re hunting for a difference between the groups, but this one closes a gap instead of opening it. If warranty buyers had used their vacuums less, that could explain fewer repairs. Ruling that out helps the director. Wrong direction.

questions.stimulus: Every acquisition paid for from the Varden Museum’s endowment fund must first be approved by the collections committee, and the committee approves only works that will be put on public display. The museum’s proposed purchase, a fragile medieval manuscript, would be kept permanently in a storage vault open only to staff. Thus, the manuscript cannot be bought with endowment money.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any work that is on public display can be viewed by people who are not members of the museum’s staff.
Some acquisitions paid for from the endowment fund have never actually been put on public display.
The collections committee has approved every proposed acquisition it has reviewed that would be put on public display.
The manuscript would interest visiting scholars far more than ordinary visitors.
If a proposed acquisition would be put on public display, it can be paid for from the endowment fund.
questions.explanation: The chain is: endowment funding requires committee approval, and committee approval requires public display. The missing link connects “kept permanently in a vault open only to staff” to “not on public display.” (A) supplies it in contrapositive form: whatever is on public display can be seen by non-staff, so the manuscript would not be on display, cannot get approval, and therefore cannot be bought with endowment money. (C) and (E) reverse the conditionals and say what is enough for approval or funding, which cannot show that the purchase is barred. (B) links the manuscript to nothing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The manuscript cannot be bought with endowment money.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Endowment funding → committee approval; committee approval → public display; the manuscript would be kept permanently in a staff-only vault.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: endowment-funded → committee-approved → on public display. Contrapositive: not on display → not approved → not endowment-funded. To get the conclusion, we need the manuscript to be not on public display. The premise only says it would sit permanently in a vault open only to staff. Missing link: staff-only vault → not on public display. Plug that in and the chain runs all the way to "can't be bought with endowment money."

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the missing link stated as a contrapositive: on public display → viewable by non-staff. Flip it: viewable only by staff → not on public display. The manuscript stays in a staff-only vault, so it isn't on display, so it isn't approved, so it can't be endowment-funded. The conclusion follows with certainty. Don't let the backward-looking wording hide it.

So? Even if some past purchases slipped past the display requirement, that says nothing about this manuscript, and it certainly doesn't help prove the purchase is barred. If anything, it hints the rules aren't always followed.
This reverses the second rule. It says on display → approved, which is the sufficient direction for getting approval. We need something that blocks approval, not something that grants it.
Who would be interested is irrelevant to the conditional rules. Doesn't link the manuscript to public display.
Reversed. On display → can be funded. That tells you what's enough to qualify, not what disqualifies. Doesn't get you to "cannot."

questions.stimulus: At an animal shelter, cats housed in the quiet rooms have long been adopted more quickly than cats housed in the noisy main kennel area. Last fall, hoping to speed adoptions, the shelter soundproofed another room and moved half of its main-area cats into it. Yet the cats that were moved were not adopted any more quickly than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why moving the cats did not shorten their adoption times?
choices: Cats in the main kennel area are frequently exposed to the noise of dogs barking in a nearby wing of the shelter.
Most people who adopt cats from the shelter visit on weekends, when the shelter is at its busiest and noisiest.
Unlike the other quiet rooms, which open onto the lobby, the new room is reached through a staff corridor that visitors seldom enter.
Some main-area cats have been adopted within a day of arriving.
The newly soundproofed room is larger and brighter than any of the other quiet rooms at the shelter.
questions.explanation: Quiet rooms seemed to speed adoptions, yet moving cats into a new quiet room did nothing. (C) shows that the old quiet rooms had another advantage the new room lacks: visitors pass them on the way in. If adopters rarely see the cats in the new room, quiet alone would not help. (E) and (A) deepen the puzzle, and (B) and (D) do not distinguish the moved cats from any others.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Cats in quiet rooms get adopted faster, but cats moved into a newly quieted room did not get adopted any faster.

breakdown.analysis: Maybe quiet was never the whole story. What else might the old quiet rooms have had going for them? Location, visibility, who walks past. We need a difference between the old quiet rooms and the new one that would matter to adopters.

choices.note: Deepens the puzzle. If the main area is even noisier than we thought, moving cats out of it should have helped more.
Applies to every cat in the shelter. It doesn’t explain why the moved cats in particular gained nothing.

CORRECT. The old quiet rooms sit where every visitor walks in; the new one is tucked behind a staff corridor. Adopters can’t choose cats they never see, so the moved cats got quiet without the exposure. Both facts now fit.
Irrelevant. Some fast adoptions from the noisy area don’t explain why the move failed to help.
Tempting, because it’s about the new room. But a larger, brighter room should make the cats more appealing, so this makes the result more puzzling.

questions.stimulus: Surveys consistently find that readers of mystery novels say what they most enjoy is a plot they cannot predict. Yet nearly all of the mysteries that these same readers rate as most enjoyable follow one of a handful of familiar formulas. So these readers must be mistaken about what they enjoy.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on survey responses from readers who may not be representative of the much larger population of mystery readers
confuses readers’ enjoyment of a novel with their admiration for the skill of its author
overlooks the possibility that some readers of mystery novels enjoy plots they can predict at least as much as plots they cannot
infers that formulaic mysteries are popular merely from the fact that so many of them are published
takes for granted that a novel built on a familiar formula has a plot readers can foresee
questions.explanation: The argument slides from “follows a familiar formula” to “has a predictable plot.” A mystery can follow a standard formula and still keep readers from guessing the outcome, so the ratings need not conflict with the survey answers. (E) names that shift. (A) is the textbook trap, but the conclusion concerns only the surveyed readers; (C) is consistent with the argument; (B) and (D) describe reasoning the argument never uses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mystery readers are mistaken about what they enjoy.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: They say they most enjoy unpredictable plots; the mysteries they rate highest follow familiar formulas.

breakdown.analysis: Is a formula the same as a predictable plot? Every mystery follows the same outline: crime, clues, suspects, reveal. Readers still can’t guess who did it. The argument needs “formulaic” to mean “predictable,” and it doesn’t. It’s like saying people who claim to love surprises can’t really, since they love birthday parties, which always follow the same script.

choices.note: Tempting, because surveys invite this objection. But the conclusion is about “these readers,” the same people whose ratings are cited. No generalization, so no sampling problem.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Readers who answered our online poll love mysteries, so most adults love mysteries.

choices.note: Admiration for the author never comes up.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Readers praise this author’s craft, so they must enjoy reading her books.

choices.note: Not a flaw. If some readers enjoy predictable plots, that fits the argument’s conclusion rather than undermining it.
The argument relies on readers’ ratings, not on how many formulaic books get published.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Bookstores are full of formula mysteries, so readers must love them.

choices.note: CORRECT. The whole argument depends on equating a familiar formula with a plot readers can foresee. Without that, high ratings for formulaic books fit perfectly well with a love of unpredictable plots.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Last month we published a leaked draft of the city’s zoning report. We had confirmed that the draft was authentic, and our story quoted it accurately, but the planning office had already corrected several of its figures, and we did not check with that office before publishing. Many readers came away believing the uncorrected figures. So we were wrong to publish the story as we did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor’s reasoning?
choices: A newspaper should not publish a story based on a leaked document unless it has first confirmed that the document is authentic.
Faithfully reproducing one’s material does not clear a publication that misleads its audience, if a check it neglected to make would have exposed the problem.
A newspaper should prominently correct any story that has misled its readers.
A newspaper is not at fault for a false impression created by a story if the story accurately reports the contents of an authentic document.
Government offices that correct figures in public reports should announce those corrections widely enough that the press is unlikely to repeat the original figures.
questions.explanation: The editor concedes that the draft was authentic and accurately quoted but still judges the story wrong, because readers were misled and the paper never checked with the planning office. (B) makes that combination enough for fault in general terms: faithful reproduction does not clear a publication that misleads its audience when a neglected check would have exposed the problem. (A) is the trap: it echoes “authentic,” but the paper met that condition, so (A) cannot show it did wrong. (C) concerns what to do afterward, (D) would excuse the paper, and (E) addresses the government, not the newspaper.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The paper was wrong to publish the story as it did.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The paper confirmed the draft was authentic and quoted it accurately; the figures had already been corrected; the paper didn’t check with the planning office; readers were misled.

breakdown.analysis: The editor admits the story was accurate. So why was it wrong? Because the paper skipped a check it could have made, and readers ended up believing bad numbers. A principle-justify answer has to tell you that this situation counts as wrong. Prephrase: being accurate about a document isn’t enough if you mislead people by skipping a check you could have made.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s about leaked documents and uses the word “authentic.” But the paper satisfied this rule: it confirmed the draft was authentic. A rule the paper obeyed can’t show it did wrong.

CORRECT. Readers were misled; the paper skipped a check that was available (the planning office) and would have exposed the corrected figures. Under this principle, the paper's faithful quoting doesn't clear it, so the story was wrong as published. Every condition matches the facts, just in more general words.
Right topic, wrong verdict. This tells the paper what to do after the fact. It says nothing about whether publishing was wrong in the first place.
Opposite. The story accurately reported an authentic document, so this principle would clear the paper.
Wrong party. This puts the duty on the government office. Even if the office fell short, that doesn’t make the newspaper wrong.

questions.stimulus: Tree-ring analysis of the oak beams that support the roof of a medieval granary shows that the trees from which the beams were cut were all felled in 1438. Since a beam cannot be put in place before its tree has been felled, the granary cannot have been built before 1438.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that the beams may have been cut and stored for many years before they were put in place
takes for granted that tree-ring analysis can determine the year in which a tree was felled
presumes, without providing justification, that the granary was built in 1438
overlooks the possibility that the beams were salvaged from an older building and reused in the granary
overlooks the possibility that the part of the structure that was dated is younger than the rest of it
questions.explanation: The argument dates the whole granary by its roof beams. If the roof was added or replaced after the walls went up, the granary could predate 1438. (E) states this. (A) and (D) sound like standard dating problems, but each would make the building the same age or younger than the beams, which fits the conclusion that it is no older than 1438. (B) objects to a premise, and (C) overstates the conclusion, which sets only a lower limit.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The granary cannot have been built before 1438.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The roof beams come from trees felled in 1438; a beam can’t be installed before its tree is felled.

breakdown.analysis: The beams can’t be older than 1438 in the building. Fine. But are the beams as old as the building? Roofs get replaced. A 1438 roof on a 1390 building is no contradiction. Notice the conclusion’s direction: “not before 1438.” Anything that would make the building later than the beams fits the conclusion. Only something that makes it earlier hurts.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Storage is a real dating problem, but it pushes the building date later, past 1438. The conclusion says only “not before 1438,” so this fits it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The timber was felled in 1438, so the house was built in 1438.

choices.note: Premise objection. The argument is entitled to its dating evidence; the flaw is in what it does with it.
Overstated. The argument sets a floor (no earlier than 1438), not an exact year.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The beams date to 1438, so the granary went up that year.

choices.note: Sounds like the right worry, but reused beams were still felled in 1438, so the building still can’t predate 1438. It doesn’t hurt this conclusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The beams are older than 1438, so the barn must be too.

choices.note: CORRECT. The roof may be a later addition or replacement. The beams date the roof, not necessarily the walls, so the granary as a whole could be older than 1438.

questions.stimulus: Food critic: A restaurant’s reputation for freshness depends on its use of ingredients that are in season. But a restaurant that builds its menu entirely around seasonal ingredients must change that menu several times a year, and frequent menu changes make it hard for a kitchen to prepare dishes consistently. Moreover, diners seldom return to a restaurant whose dishes are inconsistent. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: no restaurant can have both a reputation for freshness and a loyal base of repeat customers
a menu made up only of seasonal dishes can jeopardize a restaurant’s hold on its repeat customers
restaurants that hope to attract repeat customers should avoid using seasonal ingredients in their dishes
a reputation for consistency may well matter more to a restaurant’s success than a reputation for freshness does
restaurants that cook consistently seldom use in-season ingredients
questions.explanation: The premises connect an all-seasonal menu to frequent changes, frequent changes to difficulty with consistency, and inconsistency to diners not returning, so the cautious conclusion in (B) follows, phrased in new words. (A) is the attractive overreach: the critic says only that consistency is hard, not impossible. (C) adds a recommendation the premises do not support, (D) is hedged but still ranks two reputations the critic never compares, and (E) reverses the direction of the reasoning.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) A freshness reputation depends on using in-season ingredients; 2) an all-seasonal menu must change several times a year; 3) frequent menu changes make consistency hard; 4) diners seldom return to restaurants with inconsistent dishes.

breakdown.analysis: Follow the chain: all-seasonal menu → frequent changes → consistency is hard → (if inconsistent) diners seldom return. Notice the soft spot: "hard," not "impossible." So the honest ending is a risk, not a certainty. Prephrase: a restaurant with an all-seasonal menu risks losing repeat customers. Match the strength of the conclusion to the strength of the premises.

choices.note: Too strong. "Hard" isn't "impossible," and a restaurant can lean on seasonal ingredients without building its entire menu around them. "No restaurant can" overreaches.

CORRECT. It follows the chain in different words and keeps the right strength. An all-seasonal menu makes consistency hard, and inconsistency drives diners away, so such a menu puts repeat business at risk. “Can jeopardize” is as strong as the premises allow, and no stronger.
A recommendation the premises don't support. The problem is building the menu entirely around seasonal ingredients, not using any at all.

Hedged, but still unsupported. "May well matter more" is a comparison of value, and the critic never weighs freshness against consistency. Don't pick an answer just because it's cautious; a soft claim about something the premises never address is still unsupported.
This reverses the chain. The premises go from seasonal to inconsistent, not from consistent back to seasonal. Plenty of consistent restaurants could use seasonal ingredients in part of the menu.

questions.stimulus: Brightline advertises that its LED bulbs last 20 years, a figure based on tests of bulbs in open fixtures at room temperature. But heat shortens the life of LED bulbs, and most household light fixtures are enclosed, trapping heat around the bulb. So in most households, Brightline bulbs will last well short of 20 years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Brightline’s competitors test their bulbs under more realistic conditions.
Trapped heat in enclosed fixtures is the main cause of the LED bulb failures that occur in most households.
Brightline knew, when it first advertised the 20-year figure, that its bulbs would not last nearly that long in most of the homes where they would be used.
Bulbs installed in enclosed fixtures fail sooner than bulbs installed in any other kind of household light fixture.
Brightline bulbs are not designed in a way that protects them from the heat trapped in enclosed fixtures.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from a general fact, that heat shortens LED life, to a prediction about Brightline bulbs in particular. If Brightline bulbs were built to withstand the heat of enclosed fixtures, that prediction would fail, so the argument requires (E). (B) is tempting but too strong: heat need only shorten these bulbs’ lives significantly, not be the leading cause of failure. (D) and (C) are likewise more than the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: In most households, Brightline bulbs will last well short of 20 years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The 20-year claim comes from tests in open fixtures at room temperature; heat shortens LED life; most household fixtures are enclosed and trap heat.

breakdown.analysis: Does a general fact about LEDs have to apply to these LEDs? The argument moves from "heat shortens LED life" to a prediction about Brightline bulbs. That works only if Brightline bulbs are like typical LEDs in this respect. If Brightline built in a heat sink that shrugs off enclosed-fixture heat, the prediction fails. It's like saying "sun fades fabric, so this awning will fade" without checking whether it's UV-treated. We need an answer that says Brightline bulbs aren't protected. Use the negation test on each choice.

choices.note: Negate it: competitors' tests are just as unrealistic. The argument about Brightline is unaffected. Not required.
choices.negation: Brightline’s competitors do not test their bulbs under more realistic conditions.

choices.note: Too strong. Heat only needs to shorten Brightline bulbs' lives a lot, not be the number one cause of failure. Negated, something else is the main cause, but heat could still cut lifespans well short of 20 years. Argument survives.
choices.negation: Trapped heat in enclosed fixtures is not the main cause of the LED bulb failures that occur in most households.

choices.note: Intent doesn't matter. The argument is about how long the bulbs last, not whether Brightline knew. Negated, an honest mistake, and the conclusion stands.
choices.negation: Brightline did not know, when it first advertised the 20-year figure, that its bulbs would fall well short of that in most homes.

choices.note: Too strong. Enclosed fixtures don't have to be the worst kind, just hot enough to shorten life. Negated, some other fixture is even worse, and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: Bulbs installed in enclosed fixtures do not fail sooner than bulbs installed in every other kind of household light fixture.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, Brightline bulbs are designed to resist enclosed-fixture heat. Then the general fact about heat wouldn't apply to them, and the prediction collapses. Negation wrecks the argument, so it's required.
choices.negation: Brightline bulbs are designed in a way that protects them from the heat trapped in enclosed fixtures.

questions.stimulus: In a certain mountain region, every bird species that feeds mainly on seeds nests on the ground, and every species that nests on the ground migrates south for the winter. Several of the region’s songbird species, however, remain in the region throughout the winter.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: At least one of the region’s songbird species does not rely chiefly on seeds for its food.
No songbird species in the region nests on the ground.
Every bird species in the region that migrates south for the winter nests on the ground.
Some of the bird species in the region that feed mainly on seeds are songbirds.
Most of the region’s bird species that stay through the winter feed mainly on insects rather than seeds.
questions.explanation: Seeds → ground nesting → migration. The songbirds that stay all winter do not migrate, so they do not nest on the ground and do not feed mainly on seeds. Since several such species exist, (A) must be true. (B) overreaches to all songbirds, (C) reverses a conditional, (D) could be false, and (E) brings in insects, which the statements never mention.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Feeds mainly on seeds → nests on ground; 2) nests on ground → migrates; 3) several songbird species stay all winter (don’t migrate).

breakdown.analysis: Chain: seeds → ground → migrates. Contrapositive: doesn’t migrate → doesn’t nest on ground → doesn’t feed mainly on seeds. The only concrete things we’re told exist are the songbirds that stay. Run them through the contrapositive and you get: some songbirds don’t live mainly on seeds.

choices.note: CORRECT. The songbirds that stay don’t migrate, so they don’t nest on the ground, so they don’t feed mainly on seeds. Several exist, so at least one songbird species doesn’t rely chiefly on seeds.
Too strong. The songbirds that stay don’t nest on the ground, but songbirds that migrate might.
Reverses rule 2. Ground nesters migrate; that doesn’t make every migrant a ground nester.
Could be true, but nothing requires it. There may be no seed-eating songbirds at all.
New information. Insects never come up, and “most” is unsupported.

questions.stimulus: Animal behaviorist: When a pet parrot starts plucking out its own feathers, owners typically assume it is bored and buy it more toys. They would do better to consult an avian veterinarian first. In many cases, plucking has a nutritional rather than a psychological cause: it often begins in parrots that already have plenty of toys and companionship, and it frequently stops after a change in the bird’s diet.
questions.stem: The claim that in many cases plucking has a nutritional rather than a psychological cause plays which one of the following roles in the animal behaviorist’s argument?
choices: It is the argument’s main conclusion, and the observations about toys, companionship, and diet are offered in support of it.
It is a view that the argument presents in order to call it into question by citing evidence that conflicts with it.
It is supported by the observations about toys and diet, and it is in turn offered as grounds for the advice to owners.
It is a premise offered in support of the view that parrots that pluck their own feathers are usually bored rather than poorly nourished.
It is a hypothesis that the argument advances to explain why owners of parrots that pluck tend to buy more toys.
questions.explanation: The main conclusion is the unflagged advice in the middle: owners would do better to consult an avian veterinarian first. The nutritional claim is the reason given for that advice, and it is itself supported by the observations about toys and diet that follow the colon, so it is an intermediate conclusion, as (C) says. (A) is the trap: the claim comes last and reads like a thesis, but it is offered as the reason to see a veterinarian, not the other way round. (B) and (E) misdescribe the claim, and (D) has it supporting the boredom view it opposes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Owners of parrots that pluck would do better to consult an avian veterinarian before buying more toys.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Plucking often begins in parrots that already have toys and company, and often stops after a diet change; so in many cases it has a nutritional cause; so see a veterinarian first.

breakdown.analysis: Where's the conclusion? Not at the end, and nothing flags it. Ask which statement supports which. Why should owners see a vet first? Because the cause is often nutritional. Why think the cause is nutritional? Because of the toy and diet observations. So the chain is: 1. observations → 2. nutritional cause → 3. see a vet first. The claim in the stem is the middle link: supported, and supporting. Most students pick (A) because the claim comes last, gets direct support after the colon, and sounds like the thesis. It fails because the advice to owners is what the nutritional claim is there to justify. Lesson: position and tone don't make a main conclusion; the support relations do.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The claim sits at the end and gets direct support, so it feels like the point. But ask why the behaviorist tells us the cause is nutritional: to show owners should see a vet before buying toys. That advice is the main conclusion, and it rests on this claim, not the other way round.
Opposite. The argument doesn't question this claim; it argues for it. The view it calls into question is the owners' boredom assumption.
CORRECT. The toy and diet observations support it, and it supports the advice to see a vet first. A claim that is supported and then used as support is an intermediate (subsidiary) conclusion.
Wrong relation. The nutritional claim cuts against the boredom view; it doesn't support it.
The claim explains feather plucking, not owners' toy buying. Wrong thing explained.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: It is wrong to break a promise unless keeping it would seriously harm someone who had no part in making it. Consider a woman who promised to sell her car to her brother and then learned that the sale would seriously harm her elderly neighbor, who had no say in the promise and depends on rides in that car to reach medical appointments. So she would not be wrong to break her promise.
questions.stem: The ethicist’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: One does nothing wrong in going back on one’s word if honoring it would gravely harm a third party.
A promise whose keeping would harm no outsider must be kept, however inconvenient keeping it may be.
The woman’s brother would not be seriously harmed if she broke her promise to sell him the car.
No one should make a promise without first considering how keeping it might affect people who are not party to it.
The harm the neighbor would suffer from the sale is greater than any harm the brother would suffer if the promise were broken.
questions.explanation: The ethicist’s principle says only when breaking a promise is wrong: whenever no outsider would be seriously harmed. The woman’s case falls under the exception, but an exception to a rule of wrongness does not by itself make an act permissible. (A) supplies the missing direction in new terms: if keeping one’s word would gravely harm a third party, breaking it is not wrong. (B) restates the principle the ethicist already gave, (C) and (E) add facts about the brother that no stated rule connects to permissibility, and (D) concerns making promises, not breaking them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The woman would not be wrong to break her promise.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Principle: no serious harm to an outsider → breaking is wrong; keeping this promise would seriously harm an outsider (the neighbor).

breakdown.analysis: “Wrong unless H” means: not H → wrong. Here H is true. So what? The rule only tells us when breaking is wrong; it is silent when H holds. Concluding “not wrong” from H is negating the rule. Classic. We need the other direction: H → not wrong. Think of “you can’t enter unless you have a ticket.” Having a ticket doesn’t guarantee entry.

choices.note: CORRECT. Honoring the promise would gravely harm a third party → breaking it is not wrong. The neighbor had no say in the promise, so he is a third party, and the sale would seriously harm him. So breaking the promise is not wrong, which is the conclusion. It supplies exactly the direction the stated principle lacks, in different words.
Tempting, because it sounds like a principle about promises. But it just restates the ethicist’s rule (no outsider harmed → must keep). It says nothing about cases where an outsider is harmed.
Tempting. It removes one worry about breaking. But no stated principle says breaking is permissible when the promisee isn’t harmed, so the conclusion still doesn’t follow.
Right topic, wrong question. This is about making promises, not about whether breaking one is wrong.
Weighing the harms is natural, but nothing tells us that a greater harm to the outsider makes breaking permissible. Without that rule, the comparison leads nowhere.

questions.stimulus: Orchestra manager: Critics claim that moving our community orchestra’s weekly rehearsal from Saturday morning to Sunday evening has hurt rehearsal attendance, since rehearsals now run late into a night before a workday. But this complaint is unfounded. The number of musicians on the orchestra’s roster this season is actually slightly higher than it was last season, before the change.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, weakens the orchestra manager’s argument EXCEPT:
choices: The orchestra no longer removes musicians from its roster for missing rehearsals, as it routinely did in past seasons.
Many musicians who once stayed for every rehearsal now regularly leave at the break so that they can get home at a reasonable hour before work.
Since the change, section leaders have often had to rehearse with several chairs empty, which rarely happened when rehearsals were on Saturday mornings.
Most of this season’s rehearsals have not ended until well after ten o’clock on Sunday night.
Many musicians who joined this season did so mainly to qualify for a conservatory scholarship that requires membership in an ensemble but not attendance at its rehearsals.
questions.explanation: The manager answers a complaint about rehearsal attendance with a figure about roster size. (A) and (E) show that the roster can grow without attendance growing, (B) shows attendance itself suffering from the late hour, and (C) reports empty chairs at rehearsals, which is direct evidence that attendance fell. (D) merely confirms the critics’ premise that rehearsals run late, which the manager never disputes; it gives no evidence that anyone stopped attending, so it does not weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics’ complaint that the schedule change hurt rehearsal attendance is unfounded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: This season slightly more musicians are on the roster than last season, before the change.

breakdown.analysis: So what if more people are on the roster? The complaint is about showing up to rehearsal. Roster size and attendance are different things. Four answers will pry those apart or attack the roster number itself; one won't. Watch out for the answer that just repeats the critics' premise: the manager never said rehearsals don't run late, so confirming it doesn't hurt him. It's like a gym owner saying "we have more members than ever" when asked whether people still come in to work out.

choices.note: Weakens. If musicians stay on the roster even when they skip rehearsals, a bigger roster tells you nothing about attendance.
Weakens directly. This is the harm the critics described: the late hour is cutting rehearsals short for musicians who used to stay.
Weakens directly. Empty chairs at rehearsal, which were rare under the old schedule, are evidence that attendance actually dropped, whatever the roster says.

CORRECT. It does not weaken. This just confirms the critics' premise that rehearsals run late. The manager never denied that; his claim is that no harm to attendance followed. Nothing here shows anyone stopped coming. Tempting because it sounds like the critics' side.
Weakens. These new members joined for a reason that doesn't require showing up, so the roster increase can come with no rise, or a fall, in attendance.

questions.stimulus: Many sections of sidewalk that a city poured last year have developed cracks. The city’s engineer attributes the cracking to a cheaper concrete mix that the city’s supplier began providing early last year, rather than to the unusually harsh winter that followed, noting that the cracked sections contain far less of the binding agent that helps concrete resist strain.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the engineer’s argument?
choices: Sections poured with the new mix early last year began cracking during the summer, months before any freezing weather.
Concrete that freezes repeatedly before it has fully cured is especially likely to crack within its first year.
Concrete containing less binding agent tends to be weaker than concrete of the same type that contains more of it.
The supplier did not tell the city that it had switched mixes.
Some sidewalk sections that the city poured several years ago, before the supplier changed mixes, also cracked last winter.
questions.explanation: The engineer blames the mix rather than the winter, so the strongest support rules out the winter. (A) does that through timing: cracks in new-mix sections appeared before any freezing weather. (C) is the trap: it merely restates what the engineer already says about the binding agent and does nothing to separate the mix from the winter. (B) and (E) point toward the winter, and (D) concerns how the change was handled, not what caused the cracks.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The cracking was caused by the cheaper mix, not by the harsh winter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The supplier switched to a cheaper mix early last year; the cracked sections have far less binding agent, which helps concrete resist strain.

breakdown.analysis: Two suspects: the new mix and the hard winter. Both came along at about the same time, so the engineer’s evidence fits either one. What would clear the winter? Evidence that the cracks showed up before the cold arrived. Prephrase: something that rules out the winter or ties the cracks to the mix alone.

choices.note: CORRECT. If new-mix sections were already cracking in summer, the winter can’t be the cause of those cracks. Timing eliminates the rival explanation and leaves the mix.
Weakens. This gives the winter a way to cause cracks in new concrete, which helps the rival explanation.

Tempting, because it backs up the engineer’s own point. But the stimulus already says the binding agent helps concrete resist strain. Saying it again doesn’t separate the mix from the winter. Corroborating a premise adds almost nothing.
Interesting fact, but irrelevant. How the supplier communicated has nothing to do with what caused the cracks.
Weakens if anything. Old-mix sections cracked last winter too, which points toward the winter rather than the mix.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: A certain salamander species is found only in caves, yet its tiny eyes still contain working cells whose sole function is to detect light. Producing and maintaining such cells uses energy, so natural selection tends to eliminate them in animals that never encounter light. It follows that these salamanders must spend at least part of their lives where some light reaches them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the biologist’s argument?
choices: The species has lived in caves long enough for natural selection to have removed a costly trait it had no use for.
These salamanders could not survive for long in any part of a cave that no light from outside the cave ever reaches.
Any animal whose eyes contain working light-detecting cells makes use of those cells at some point in its life.
The eyes of these salamanders are much smaller than the eyes of the salamander species that live outside caves in the same region.
Producing light-detecting cells requires more energy than producing most of the other kinds of cells in a salamander’s body.
questions.explanation: The biologist infers light exposure from the persistence of light-detecting cells, on the ground that selection removes such cells when they are useless. That works only if selection has had time to act; if the species moved into darkness recently, the cells could simply be left over. (A) rules out that alternative, which the stimulus never mentions. (C) is the trap: it would make the argument work, but its negation (some animal somewhere has unused cells) does not touch this species. (B) is too strong, (E) need not hold for selection to favor losing a costly trait, and (D) is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: These salamanders spend at least part of their lives where some light reaches them.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: They live only in caves but still have working light-detecting cells; such cells cost energy; selection tends to eliminate them in animals that never encounter light.

breakdown.analysis: Why else might the cells still be there? Maybe selection just hasn’t finished the job. “Tends to eliminate” takes time. If the species moved into total darkness only recently, leftover cells prove nothing about light. It’s like inferring that someone still drives because there’s a car in the garage, when they may have stopped driving last week and haven’t sold it yet. We need an answer that rules out the “not enough time” explanation. Use the negation test.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the species hasn’t lived in caves long enough for selection to have removed an unused trait. Then the cells could persist in total darkness, and the argument collapses. A defender answer against an alternative the stimulus never raises.
choices.negation: The species has not lived in caves long enough for natural selection to have removed a costly trait it had no use for.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument says only that they spend part of their lives near some light. Negate it: they could survive in total darkness. The argument is fine; surviving there doesn’t mean they never visit light.
choices.negation: These salamanders could survive for long in some part of a cave that no light from outside ever reaches.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Assume it and the conclusion follows, so it feels like the bridge. But it’s a sweeping claim about every animal. Negate it: some animal, somewhere, has working cells it never uses. That says nothing about this species, so the argument survives. Sufficient, not required.
choices.negation: Some animal whose eyes contain working light-detecting cells never makes use of them.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Eye size doesn’t bear on whether the cells are used. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: The eyes of these salamanders are not much smaller than those of the salamander species that live outside caves in the same region.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs only that the cells cost some energy, which the stimulus already says. Negate it: they cost less than most other cells. They still cost something, so selection can still favor losing them.
choices.negation: Producing light-detecting cells does not require more energy than producing most other kinds of salamander cells.

questions.stimulus: Every candidate who has won the party’s nomination for governor in recent decades had either served in the state legislature or held statewide office. The current front-runner has never held statewide office, but she did serve two terms in the legislature. So she will win this year’s nomination.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Every novel that has won the prize in recent years was either a debut or a work of historical fiction. This year’s favorite is not a debut, but it is a work of historical fiction. So its winning would not break with the prize’s recent record.

Most restaurants that have earned the guide’s top rating in recent years either employed a classically trained chef or grew their own produce. One new restaurant grows its own produce but has no such chef. So it will probably earn the top rating.

Ilse Varga’s documentary will take the festival’s top award this year. True, Varga has directed films before. But the documentary was shot entirely abroad, and lately no film has taken that award without having been either shot abroad or made by a first-time director.

Every architect who has won the city’s design award in recent years had previously designed a public library. One of this year’s entrants has designed two public libraries. So she will win this year’s design award.

Every runner who has won the marathon in recent years trained either at high altitude or with a professional coach. One of this year’s entrants will not win. So she trained neither at high altitude nor with a professional coach.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a condition every past winner met (legislature or statewide office) as enough to win, noting that the candidate lacks one option but has the other. (C) has every element, rearranged: the prediction comes first, the denied option is stated as “has directed films before,” and the either/or rule appears last as “no film has taken that award without.” (A) is the trap: it copies the original almost word for word, but its conclusion (winning would not break the record) is only that winning is consistent with the pattern, which follows validly. (D) commits the same basic error but has no either/or structure; (B) hedges with “most” and “probably”; (E) reasons from not winning, a different error.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The front-runner will win the nomination.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every recent winner had B or C; she lacks C but has B.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All past winners had B or C; X lacks C but has B; so X will win. (A necessary condition treated as sufficient, dressed in an either/or.)

breakdown.analysis: Having what every winner had doesn't make you a winner. Lots of former legislators lose. The either/or and the "never held statewide office" are window dressing; the flaw is necessary-treated-as-sufficient. But a parallel-flaw answer has to match the dressing too, and the certainty level. Don't match on wording. Translate each choice into the pattern first: "no film has won without X or Y" is just "every winner had X or Y," and "has directed films before" is "not a first-time director." And check what each conclusion actually claims: "would not break with the record" is a much weaker claim than "will win."

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It reads almost exactly like the original: same either/or, same denied and affirmed options. But look at the conclusion. It only says winning would fit the pattern, and that's true: the favorite has one of the two features every winner had. That's valid, so it can't parallel a flawed argument.
Close, but the certainty differs: “most” past winners and a “probably” conclusion. The original says “every” and “will.” One element changed.

CORRECT. Translate it: every recent winner was shot abroad or by a first-time director (that's what "no film has taken that award without" means); Varga isn't a first-time director; the film was shot abroad; so it will win. Same either/or, same denied and affirmed options, same certain prediction, same flaw. Only the order and the wording are disguised.
Tempting. It commits the same basic flaw (has what winners had, so will win), but there's no either/or and no denied option. When one answer matches every element, the stripped-down version loses.
A different error. This reasons from not winning to lacking the conditions, which mistakes a necessary condition the other way. The original reasons from having the condition to winning.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Supporters of a proposed tax credit for small manufacturers claim that it will boost hiring, because a similar credit in a neighboring country did so. But manufacturers there sell most of their goods abroad, while ours sell mainly at home, so that country’s results tell us little about what would happen here. It is therefore unlikely that the credit would boost hiring by our manufacturers.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the economist’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on a comparison between two countries that differ in a respect that bears on the conclusion being drawn
presumes, without providing justification, that where manufacturers sell their goods is the only factor that affects how many workers they hire
draws a conclusion about every industry from evidence that concerns manufacturers alone
treats the weakness of the support offered for a prediction as grounds for regarding that prediction as improbable
takes for granted that the rise in hiring in the other country resulted from the credit rather than from its manufacturers’ heavy reliance on foreign sales
questions.explanation: The economist shows only that the evidence from the other country is weak. That leaves the prediction unsupported, not improbable, yet the economist concludes that the credit is unlikely to boost hiring. (D) describes that move abstractly. (A) is the trap: a comparison between dissimilar countries is the supporters’ flaw, which the economist points out rather than commits. The economist does not claim where goods are sold is the only factor (B), does not take for granted what caused the other country’s results (E), and draws a conclusion only about manufacturers (C).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: It is unlikely that the credit would boost hiring by our manufacturers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Supporters rely on the neighboring country; manufacturers there sell mostly abroad while ours sell mainly at home; so that country’s results tell us little about what would happen here.

breakdown.analysis: Fine, the other country tells us little. So what does that leave us with? No good evidence either way. "We don't know" isn't "probably not." It's like saying: your only reason to think it'll rain is a forecast for another city, so it probably won't rain here. Knocking out a reason is not the same as proving the opposite. Watch the word "unlikely": it sounds modest, but it still goes beyond what the economist has shown. Prephrase: treats undermining the evidence as evidence against the claim.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. A comparison between countries that differ is a real flaw, but it's the supporters' flaw. The economist is the one pointing it out. This describes the argument the economist attacks, not the economist's own.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A tax credit boosted hiring in a country whose manufacturers export most of their goods, so it will boost hiring here too.

choices.note: The economist says where goods are sold is a relevant difference, not the only thing that affects hiring. One relevant difference is enough to weaken an analogy.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our manufacturers sell mainly at home, so nothing but finding foreign buyers could ever increase their hiring.

choices.note: The economist's conclusion is limited to our manufacturers. No generalization to every industry.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The credit won't help our manufacturers, so no industry would hire more under any tax credit.

choices.note: CORRECT. The economist undermines the support for the supporters' prediction, then treats that as a reason to think the prediction is probably false. Weak evidence for a claim leaves the claim open; it doesn't make it unlikely.
The economist never says what caused the other country's results. If anything, mentioning the export difference hints that something other than the credit might matter. Not taken for granted.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Hiring rose in the other country after its credit took effect, so the credit must be what raised it.

questions.stimulus: When the editors of an online encyclopedia came to doubt its long-standing claim about where a certain seventeenth-century mapmaker was born, they simply deleted the claim. Some users object that the deletion should have been flagged on the page. Admittedly, a flag would have cost the editors nothing. But nothing the entry now says is anything the editors question, and they replied in full to every user who wrote to ask about the change. So the editors were not obliged to flag the deletion.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: One is obliged to take a beneficial step only if taking it would cost one nothing at all.
Editors may delete a long-standing claim they doubt if the entry then asserts nothing they question and they answer every user who asks why.
Editors need not call attention to the deletion of a claim from a reference work if they have established that the deleted claim was false.
Whoever alters a source others rely on need not publicize the change if the source then asserts nothing its keeper doubts and all who inquire get answers.
Users of a reference work are entitled to be told of every change made to it, unless telling them would be costly to its editors.
questions.explanation: The disputed point is not the deletion but the missing flag, and the concession rules out cost as an excuse. The argument rests on two facts instead: the entry affirms nothing the editors doubt, and they explained the change to everyone who asked. (D) makes those two conditions enough to release anyone who alters a relied-upon source from publicizing the change, in general terms (a “source,” its “keeper,” “all who inquire”). (B) is the trap: it restates both facts almost word for word, but what it licenses is the deletion, which nobody disputes, not the decision to skip the flag. (A) turns on cost with an “only if” condition the cost-free flag satisfies, so it cannot show the editors were not obliged. (C) would excuse silence only if the claim were false, and the editors merely doubt it. (E) favors the users, since flagging costs nothing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The editors were not obliged to flag the deletion.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Concession: a flag would have cost nothing. But the entry asserts nothing the editors question, and they fully answered every user who asked.

breakdown.analysis: What exactly is in dispute? Not the deletion. The users want a flag. The author even concedes a flag would have been free, so the defense isn't about cost. It rests on two facts: nothing doubtful is asserted, and anyone who asked got a full answer. A principle-justify answer has to say that those conditions release you from announcing the change. Translate the abstract answer back into the case: "source others rely on" = the encyclopedia entry; "publicize the alteration" = flag the deletion. And beware the answer that echoes the facts perfectly but rules on the wrong question.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses the conceded fact (the flag costs nothing). But it's an "only if": costing nothing is required for an obligation, not enough to remove one. The flag meets the condition, so this can't show the editors were free of the obligation; if anything it leaves room for one.

Tempting, and the main trap. It repeats both facts nearly word for word, so it feels like a perfect fit. But read what it permits: deleting the claim. Nobody objects to the deletion; the dispute is over the missing flag, and this says nothing about flagging.
Near miss. It excuses silence when the deleted claim was false. The editors only came to doubt the claim; we don’t know it was false, so the principle doesn’t apply.

CORRECT. Translate it: the entry is a source others rely on; it now asserts nothing the editors doubt; every user who asked got a full reply, so all who inquired got answers. Under this principle, no one has to publicize the change, so the editors weren't obliged to flag the deletion. Both conditions match the facts, and the verdict matches the conclusion.
Points the other way. Flagging costs nothing, so this principle would back the objecting users.

questions.stimulus: Many researchers want a remote field station to host more visiting scientists each summer. But all of the station’s fieldwork depends on access granted by the ranchers whose land surrounds it, and they already complain that visitors disturb their cattle. If the ranchers withdrew that access, no research could be done there at all. So the station should not host more visitors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments relies on a principle most similar to the principle on which the argument above relies?
choices: A community garden should not add plots, though many residents want them. All its water comes from a neighbor’s well, and the neighbor has said that if the garden’s use grows any further, he will begin charging for the water it draws.

A small press could publish nothing if its one printer ended the credit he extends it, and he already complains that the press’s orders strain his shop. So, however many writers ask to join it, the press should not take on more authors.

A choir should not schedule more concerts, though its audiences keep growing. Several of its singers say they are already tired, and a few have said they might leave the choir if the schedule became any heavier.
A clinic should not add evening hours, though many patients want them. It depends entirely on its two physicians, and adding evening hours would require hiring a third, whom the clinic cannot afford.

A museum should not lend its most famous painting to a touring exhibition, though many people would see it there. Paintings are sometimes damaged in transit, and if this one were, it could never be replaced.
