questions.explanation: The principle: do not expand to meet demand when expansion would further strain the one party the whole enterprise depends on, since losing that party would end everything. (B) has every element, rearranged: it opens with the stakes (the press could publish nothing), names the single creditor already strained by its orders, and saves the demand for a concession inside the conclusion. Every choice reaches the same “don’t expand” verdict, so the elements decide. (A) risks only higher costs, not the end of the garden; (C) risks losing a few singers, not the choir; (D) rests on affordability, not on alienating an indispensable party; (E) involves an irreplaceable loss but no dependence on anyone.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The station should not host more visitors.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Demand is high; all fieldwork depends on the ranchers’ access; the ranchers already object to visitors; losing their access would end all research.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Expanding to meet demand would further strain the party on whom everything depends; losing that party would end the whole enterprise; so don’t expand.

breakdown.analysis: Strip out the cattle. The principle is: don’t grow if growth risks losing the one party without which you have nothing. Three pieces have to be there: demand to expand, a single indispensable party already strained, and the stakes being the whole operation. Every answer here says “don’t expand,” so the conclusion won’t help you. Check each piece.

choices.note: Tempting. Demand, a neighbor on whom the garden depends, and a threatened change. But the threat is a fee, not the end of the garden. The stakes element is broken: paying more isn’t losing everything.

CORRECT. Reorder it to match: writers want in (demand); if the one printer ends the credit, nothing gets published (total dependence, total stakes); he already says the orders strain his shop (already strained); so don't take on more authors. Every element matches, even though the pieces come in a different order and the demand shows up only as a concession.

Tempting, and the main trap. A strained group that might leave. But losing a few singers doesn’t end the choir, and the choir doesn’t depend on any one party. It’s a principle about overworking members.
Total dependence is there, but the reason not to expand is affordability: the clinic can’t pay a third doctor. Nobody is being strained into leaving.
Irreversible total loss, but no demand being balanced against a party the museum depends on. The principle here is about risking something irreplaceable.

questions.stimulus: Of the customers who bought a certain desk chair from an office-supply retailer last year, most also bought the optional lumbar cushion. Of those customers who returned the chair, however, most had not bought the cushion. No customer bought more than one chair of that model, and every return was made by a customer who had bought the chair last year.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most of the customers who bought the chair last year but did not also buy the optional lumbar cushion later returned the chair.
Buying the optional lumbar cushion made customers less likely than they otherwise would have been to return their chairs.
More of the chairs were returned by customers who bought the lumbar cushion than by customers who did not.
Most buyers of the chair did not return it.
Customers who bought the lumbar cushion kept their chairs at a higher rate than customers who did not.
questions.explanation: Most buyers took the cushion, yet most returns came from buyers who did not. A smaller group producing more returns must have a higher return rate, so cushion buyers kept their chairs at a higher rate, which is (E) stated from the other side. (B) is the trap: it reads the rate difference as the cushion’s effect, but the data show only a correlation; customers who skipped the cushion may differ in other ways. (A) and (D) need the overall return rate, which is not given, and (C) contradicts the second statement.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most buyers of the chair also bought the cushion; 2. Most customers who returned the chair had not bought the cushion; 3. One chair per customer, and every return came from last year's buyers.

breakdown.analysis: This is a rate-versus-count puzzle. Say 100 people bought the chair: 70 with the cushion, 30 without. If most returns came from the no-cushion group, that smaller group produced more returns than the bigger one. So its return rate is higher, and the cushion group's keep rate is higher. That's the safe inference, but watch the phrasing: the right answer says it from the "kept" side. Most students pick (B) because the numbers seem to show the cushion working. It fails because the facts show only a difference between groups, not a cause. Maybe people who buy add-ons are people who had already decided they love the chair.

choices.note: We don't know this. With 30 no-cushion buyers, maybe only 3 returned and 2 cushion buyers returned. Most returns would still be no-cushion, yet only 10% of that group returned.
Tempting, and the main trap. It turns a correlation into a cause. The facts show who returned chairs, not why. Buyers who skip the add-on might be less committed to the chair from the start.
This contradicts fact 2. Most returns came from customers without the cushion, so they returned more chairs.
Could be true, but nothing says so. The facts compare the two groups; they never tell us how many returns there were overall.
CORRECT. The no-cushion group is smaller (fact 1) but produced more returns (fact 2), so its return rate is higher. Flip it: cushion buyers kept their chairs at a higher rate.

passages.title: Serial Publication and the Victorian Novel
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The Pickwick Papers, which began appearing in monthly parts in 1836, helped establish a mode of publication that shaped British fiction for decades: the novel issued in installments, in separate numbers or in magazines. One literary historian has argued that many features for which Victorian novels were long faulted are best understood as products of this mode. Suspenseful endings of installments, proliferating subplots, and the habit of tagging minor characters with a signature phrase are, he argues, not lapses of craft but rational responses to what he calls “serial form.” This historian grants that some installments were stretched to fill their pages but contends that critics who dismissed such features wholesale as “padding paid for by the page” mistook the conditions of an art for its failures.

The historian’s account is persuasive in outline, but it leaves unclear what serial form demanded. In his usage the term does double duty. Sometimes it refers to the situation of readers, who met a novel in fragments weeks apart and needed reminders of who was who. At other times it refers to the situation of writers, who often composed each installment shortly before it was due and could not revise what was already in print. These are distinct pressures, and they predict different things: the first should leave its mark wherever readers encountered a text intermittently, however it was written; the second, wherever a text was written under deadline, however it was read.

His evidence, moreover, rests on a comparison whose significance he does not establish. He shows that these features are markedly more common in serialized novels than in novels first issued complete, typically in three volumes for the circulating libraries. But the comparison is telling only if the two groups are otherwise alike, and the historian simply assumes they are. If publishers offered serialization chiefly to established popular authors, whose habits of plotting predated their first serials, or to comic and sensational stories, in which suspense and broadly drawn characters were old conventions, the difference he documents may owe less to the mode of publication than to the authors and stories it attracted.

Anthony Trollope complicates matters. He usually had a novel finished before its first installment appeared, and so seldom faced a deadline. The historian nonetheless counts Trollope’s serials as confirming his thesis: Trollope still wrote knowing that readers would meet his work in parts, and by the historian’s tally those serials end installments in suspense and tag minor characters with recurring phrases as often as others do. Perhaps so—but by the same tally they contain few of the abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail that the historian also attributes to serial form. Trollope’s practice thus suggests that the two pressures his term conflates operated independently. The historian has found a real cause, then, but has not yet shown how it did its work.

passages.title: Open Balances in New England Account Books
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Account books kept by farm households in rural New England in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries record a dense traffic among neighbors: a day’s mowing, a bushel of rye, the loan of an ox team, a few yards of homespun cloth. To readers accustomed to modern commercial bookkeeping, these accounts present a puzzle. Debts between neighbors were reckoned only at long intervals, sometimes years apart, and even after a reckoning the balance was seldom paid off; it was simply carried forward into a new account. Earlier economic historians generally treated this as a symptom of scarcity—farmers postponed settlement until they had cash, which rarely came—or of bookkeeping too casual to be brought to a close.

A more persuasive explanation, suggested by anthropological studies of gift exchange, is that the open balance was not a failure of settlement but its purpose. Where households relied on one another for help at harvest, at barn raisings, and in sickness, an account closed with nothing owed on either side would have signaled that the parties no longer expected to deal with each other. A small remainder, left outstanding by design, kept the expectation of future exchange alive; it was less a debt than a standing invitation.

One study of several hundred accounts, spanning roughly half a century, from a group of hill towns in western New England lends this reading considerable support. The same households that left neighbors’ balances open settled their dealings with merchants in distant market towns promptly and to the penny. The remainders carried between neighbors were small, and over the years the balance tended to swing back and forth, so that each household was in turn creditor and debtor. And when an account between neighbors was closed exactly, town and court records from the same months frequently note a death, a removal from the town, or a lawsuit between the two families.

One account in the study shows the pattern at work. In the spring of 1792 one household lent a neighbor twelve bushels of rye; at harvest the neighbor returned thirteen, leaving the lender a bushel in debt. That winter the lender repaid the bushel with two days of threshing, work the book values at slightly more than a bushel, so that the balance swung back. The account ran on in this fashion for thirty-one years and was closed only in 1823, when a quarrel over a boundary line brought the families to court. None of this means that cash was plentiful in the hill towns; it was not. But scarcity cannot explain why the same households treated neighbors and merchants so differently. Only an explanation that attends to whom the households were dealing with can account for that difference.

passages.title: Court-Appointed Expert Witnesses
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

In a number of common-law jurisdictions, including United States federal courts, a trial judge may, on a party’s motion or on the judge’s own initiative, appoint an expert witness of the court’s choosing. The power is seldom used, and its advocates attribute this to judicial timidity. There are, however, sound reasons for the reluctance.

First, an expert introduced to the jury as the court’s own arrives cloaked in a neutrality that no party’s expert can match. Jurors told that one witness was chosen by the judge are apt to treat that witness’s opinion not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified, so that a single person who was never meant to decide the case effectively does so.

Second, the appointment itself is far from neutral. In fields where the science is unsettled—the reliability of certain forensic techniques, say, or the causes of a rare illness—competent specialists disagree, and to select one of them is to select a side. A judge, who by hypothesis lacks the expertise to resolve the dispute, is poorly placed to recognize that a choice of person is also a choice of doctrine, and the jury is unlikely ever to learn that such a choice was made.

Third, the court’s expert is shielded from the testing that adversarial procedure supplies. A lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge’s own witness risks appearing to quarrel with the judge, and few lawyers will run that risk. The remedy for partisan expertise is not to abandon the adversarial method but to strengthen it: earlier disclosure of expert reports, and pretrial hearings at which opposing experts must confront each other’s reasoning.

Passage B

Litigants do not hire experts at random. They interview several and retain the one whose views best serve their case—or whose views, for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it. The result in a technical dispute is often two confident witnesses whose conclusions are irreconcilable, presented to jurors who have no basis for choosing between them. Mock-juror studies suggest that in such contests jurors tend to credit whichever expert seems more poised and likable, a standard unrelated to the merits.

A court-appointed expert addresses this problem not by replacing the parties’ experts but by giving jurors a fixed point against which to measure them. The parties remain free to call their own witnesses and to cross-examine the court’s. And if jurors give the court’s expert more weight than either party’s, that is hardly a defect: an expert chosen for competence rather than for persuasiveness deserves more weight.

Nor need the selection be left to a judge’s unaided guesswork. Courts can ask each side to nominate candidates and appoint someone acceptable to both, or can ask a professional body to propose a panel. Where a field is genuinely divided, the appointed expert can be instructed to report the range of respectable opinion rather than only her own. And the judge should tell jurors plainly that the court’s expert, too, can be mistaken, and that they remain free to reject her testimony.

passages.title: The Missing Generations of the Freshwater Pearl Mussel
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Across much of its range in northern and western Europe, the freshwater pearl mussel, Margaritifera margaritifera, persists in rivers where it has not successfully reproduced for decades. The species is extraordinarily long-lived—individuals in some northern populations survive well over a century—and surveys that simply count mussels can therefore record a population as diminished but stable long after it has ceased to replace itself. Only when researchers began to age mussels by counting the annual growth lines in their shells did the pattern become plain: in many rivers almost no animals younger than several decades remain.

The mussel’s life cycle offers more than one point at which reproduction can fail. In summer a female releases millions of microscopic larvae, called glochidia, which survive only if they are drawn in by a young salmon or trout and clamp onto its gills. There they become encysted and live as parasites, typically for many months, before dropping off as tiny juveniles. A juvenile then spends its first several years buried in the gravel of the riverbed, where it depends on a steady flow of clean, oxygenated water through the spaces between the stones.

Two explanations of the missing generations have been advanced. One locates the failure early in the cycle, with the hosts: dams, weirs, overfishing, and dwindling salmon runs have left many rivers with too few young fish to carry the glochidia, so that juveniles are simply not being produced. The other locates it later, in the riverbed: fine sediment washed from plowed fields, drained peatland, and forestry clogs the gravel and suffocates juveniles that have been produced. Because both stresses intensified over the same decades in which recruitment ceased, the age structure of the populations cannot by itself decide between them.

Field observations bear on the question, though less decisively than is sometimes claimed. In a number of rivers, trout examined in late summer carry encysted glochidia in abundance, yet no young mussels are found in the gravel. And juveniles reared in hatcheries and placed in mesh containers in the streambed have survived well in some streams and almost not at all in others, roughly in proportion to how much fine material fills the gravel. Both findings point toward the riverbed. Yet a glochidium encysted in late summer may still be lost from its host before it matures, and because a container alters the flow of water around the animals it holds, such results carry over to wild juveniles only with caution.

The two explanations call for different remedies: restored fish passage and restocking in the one case, control of runoff from farms and forests in the other. A given river may, of course, suffer from both. Programs that rear juveniles in captivity until they are large enough to survive in the wild buy time, but they cannot tell a river’s managers which of the two remedies it needs.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The historian has shown that features of Victorian novels that earlier critics dismissed as flaws of craft were in fact rational responses to the demands of serial publication.
The historian’s account of the influence of serial publication on the Victorian novel is refuted by the case of a novelist who completed his books before serializing them.
The historian is right that serial publication shaped Victorian fiction, but his account would be sounder if it limited “serial form” to the pressures placed on writers.
Although serial publication did shape Victorian fiction, the historian’s account of that influence conflates distinct pressures and relies on a poorly controlled comparison.
The historian’s comparison of serialized novels with novels first issued complete overlooks differences between the kinds of authors and stories found in the two groups.
questions.explanation: The author grants that the historian has 'found a real cause' (last paragraph) but argues that the term 'serial form' merges two distinct pressures (second paragraph) and that the comparison behind the evidence is of uncertain significance (third paragraph); D captures the concession and both criticisms. A is the historian's own view, which the author accepts only 'in outline.' C is the near-miss: it is just as hedged, but it would restrict the term to writers, whereas the author wants the two pressures distinguished, and the Trollope case shows the reader-side pressure at work. B overstates the Trollope paragraph, which refines rather than refutes the thesis, and E is the point of the third paragraph alone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall position on the historian's thesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first sentence ('persuasive in outline, but'); paragraph 4, last sentence ('found a real cause').

breakdown.analysis: Whose view is the passage pushing? Not the historian's: he's the target. But the author isn't throwing him out either: 'persuasive in outline' and 'a real cause.' So the main point has two halves: the historian is basically right, and his account needs repair (two pressures lumped together; a shaky comparison). We need an answer with the concession and the criticism. Watch for answers that give only the historian's view or only one paragraph's complaint. One trap copies that shape exactly and slips on scope, so check what the author wants fixed.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the thesis the whole passage discusses. But it's the historian's view, stated as settled ('has shown'). The author accepts it only 'in outline' and spends three paragraphs on its problems.
Too strong. The Trollope paragraph 'complicates' the account and ends by saying the historian has found a real cause. Complicates isn't refutes.

Tempting: it has the same concession-plus-criticism content as the key. But the scope is wrong. The author doesn't want the term narrowed to writers; the complaint is that the two pressures must be told apart, and the Trollope paragraph shows the reader-side pressure doing real work.

CORRECT. 'Although serial publication did shape Victorian fiction' is the concession ('a real cause'); 'conflates distinct pressures' is paragraph 2's double-duty complaint; 'a poorly controlled comparison' is paragraph 3 (the two groups may differ in authors and stories). It paraphrases rather than repeats.
Accurate, but it's only paragraph 3. A main point has to cover the author's overall verdict, including the concession.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the comparison on which the historian’s evidence rests?
choices: Its result is consistent with the possibility that the mode of publication had little to do with the features it tallies.
It shows that serialized novels were written chiefly by established popular authors whose habits of plotting predated serialization.
Its result is mistaken, since the features in question are about as common in novels first issued complete as in serialized ones.
It would have been more telling had it included novels, such as Trollope’s, that were finished before serialization began.
It establishes that the features owe more to the authors and stories that serialization attracted than to serialization itself.
questions.explanation: In the third paragraph the author says the comparison is telling only if the two groups are otherwise alike, and that if they are not, the difference the historian documents 'may owe less to the mode of publication than to the authors and stories it attracted.' So the author holds that the comparison's result is compatible with serialization having had little effect, which is A. E is the near-miss: it turns the author's 'may' into 'establishes.' B reuses the paragraph's words but treats a hypothetical as a finding, and C contradicts the historian's result, which the author does not dispute.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer the author's view of the historian's comparison.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, especially the 'telling only if' sentence and the 'may owe less' clause.

breakdown.analysis: What's the author's complaint about the comparison? Not that the numbers are wrong: the author accepts that the features are 'markedly more common' in serials. The complaint is that the groups might differ in other ways, so the numbers might not reflect serialization at all. Prephrase: the result doesn't rule out that serialization did little. The trap is the version that says the author proved the alternative. 'May' is not 'establishes.' And don't be put off because the author elsewhere thinks the historian found 'a real cause': this question is only about what the comparison shows.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the groups differ in authors or genres, the difference 'may owe less to the mode of publication.' That's exactly saying the result is consistent with mode of publication mattering little. The hedge 'consistent with the possibility' matches the author's 'may.'
Reuses paragraph 3's words, but the author offers this only as a possibility ('If publishers offered...'), not something the comparison shows.
The author doesn't dispute the result itself; the features are 'markedly more common' in serials. The dispute is over what the result means.
Nothing suggests this. Trollope's novels were serialized, so they're already on the serialized side, and the author uses Trollope for a different point.
Too strong. The author says the difference 'may' owe more to authors and stories, not that the comparison establishes it.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the historian regards the earlier critics’ “padding paid for by the page” judgment with
choices: reluctant agreement
detached neutrality
unreserved contempt
grudging admiration
qualified rejection
questions.explanation: In the last sentence of the first paragraph, the historian 'grants that some installments were stretched to fill their pages' but contends that the critics who dismissed such features wholesale 'mistook the conditions of an art for its failures.' He rejects the judgment while conceding a grain of truth in it: qualified rejection (E). C overshoots by ignoring the concession; A overreads the concession as agreement.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the historian's (not the author's) attitude toward the 'padding' judgment.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Two parts to the sentence: a concession ('grants that some installments were stretched') and a rejection ('mistook the conditions of an art for its failures'). So: against the judgment, but not totally. Prephrase: 'disagreement with a concession.' Watch the overshoot: a word like 'contempt' throws away the 'grants.' And watch the undershoot: 'agreement' makes the concession the whole story.

choices.note: Tempting, because of 'grants.' But he grants only that some installments were stretched; the critics' judgment itself he rejects. The concession is a qualifier, not agreement.
Wrong. The historian takes a clear side: the critics 'mistook' something.
Too strong. Contempt might fit a writer who called the critics fools. The historian concedes part of their point first, so 'unreserved' is wrong.
Nothing admiring here. He says they were mistaken.
CORRECT. Rejection: the critics 'mistook the conditions of an art for its failures.' Qualified: he 'grants that some installments were stretched.'

questions.stem: In using the phrase “does double duty” (second sentence of the second paragraph), the author most probably means that the historian’s term “serial form”
choices: is applied, without distinction, to two different sets of circumstances that might have shaped the novels
serves both to explain certain features of Victorian novels and to defend those features against earlier critics
covers both novels issued in separate monthly numbers and novels serialized in magazines
is used both by the historian and by the earlier critics whose judgments about the novels he rejects
names both the characteristic features of serialized novels and the conditions that produced those features
questions.explanation: The sentences after the phrase explain it: the term sometimes refers to readers' situation and sometimes to writers' situation, which are 'distinct pressures' (second paragraph). That is A. E is the near-miss: it names two things, but features versus conditions is not the passage's distinction; both of the passage's meanings are conditions. C picks up the two modes of serialization from the first paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what two jobs the author says the term is doing.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 2-5.

breakdown.analysis: The author tells you right away: 'Sometimes it refers to the situation of readers... At other times... writers.' Two different circumstances under one name, and the author's complaint is that the historian doesn't keep them apart. Prephrase: one label, two different pressures.

choices.note: CORRECT. Readers' situation and writers' situation are the two circumstances; 'without distinction' is the author's complaint ('leaves unclear what serial form demanded').
The historian does both explain and defend, but the paragraph is about what the term refers to, not about its two uses in his argument.
Paragraph 1 mentions numbers and magazines, but that's not the double duty paragraph 2 describes.
The earlier critics never use 'serial form.' It's the historian's term ('what he calls').
Tempting: it's a 'two things' answer. But both of the passage's meanings are conditions (readers' situation, writers' situation). Features versus conditions is a split the passage never makes.

questions.stem: The author mentions “comic and sensational stories” (last sentence of the third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: point to a possible difference, other than mode of publication, between the two groups of novels the historian compares
identify the kinds of fiction for which publishers first adopted the practice of issuing novels in monthly installments
suggest that the earlier critics’ dismissal of certain features as padding was justified at least for some kinds of fiction
illustrate the pressures that serial publication placed on readers who encountered novels in fragments weeks apart
show that suspenseful endings and broadly drawn characters were more common in novels issued complete than in serialized ones
questions.explanation: The third paragraph argues that the historian's comparison is telling only if the serialized and complete novels are otherwise alike; if serialization went disproportionately to comic and sensational stories, where suspense was an old convention, genre rather than mode of publication could explain the difference. The phrase thus names a possible confounding difference (A). B turns a hypothetical into a historical claim, and E reverses the comparison.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings up comic and sensational stories.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence (the 'If publishers offered...' hypothetical).

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 3's complaint: the comparison only works if the two groups are alike in everything but publication mode. The author then names two ways they might not be: different authors, different kinds of stories. 'Comic and sensational stories' is the second. Prephrase: an alternative explanation for the difference the historian found.

choices.note: CORRECT. Genre is a difference between the groups other than mode of publication, so it could account for the features.
The sentence is an 'If'. The author doesn't claim publishers actually began with these stories; it's a possibility that would undermine the comparison.
The author doesn't side with the earlier critics. The point is about the historian's evidence, not about whether the features were padding.
Readers' pressures are paragraph 2's subject. Here the stories are about genre conventions, not reader memory.
Reverses the comparison. The historian found the features more common in serialized novels.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the historian’s interpretation of Trollope’s novels commits him to which one of the following views?
choices: The abandoned subplots found in many serialized novels arose from the conditions under which those novels were written rather than read.
The term “serial form” should be reserved for the situation of readers who met novels in installments weeks apart.
The situation of a novel’s readers can by itself account for some of the features that he attributes to serial form.
Trollope’s novels contain as many abandoned subplots and inconsistencies of detail as do novels written installment by installment.
Novelists who completed their work before serialization were more skilled at plotting than those who wrote installment by installment.
questions.explanation: The historian counts Trollope's serials as confirming his thesis on the ground that Trollope 'still wrote knowing that readers would meet his work in parts,' even though he seldom faced a deadline (fourth paragraph). Treating the suspenseful endings and recurring tags in those serials as effects of serial form therefore commits the historian to C: the readers' situation alone can produce some of those features. A is the dominant trap: it is the author's inference from Trollope's lack of abandoned subplots, a view the historian never expresses; his term 'conflates' the two pressures. B is too strong, D contradicts the fourth paragraph, and E introduces a ranking of skill no one makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the historian must believe, given his reason for counting Trollope as support. Not what the author concludes about Trollope: what the historian is stuck with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 2-3 (Trollope seldom wrote under deadline; the historian's reason for counting him anyway). Contrast sentences 4-5, which are the author talking.

breakdown.analysis: The historian's reason is the key: Trollope 'still wrote knowing that readers would meet his work in parts.' With the deadline pressure gone, the only serial pressure left is the readers' one. So if the historian says Trollope's cliffhangers and tags are serial-form effects, he's saying the reader side alone can produce them. Most students pick (A) because it is the lesson of the Trollope paragraph. It is, but it's the author's lesson. The historian's term lumps the two pressures together. Separate whose view is whose before you answer a 'commits him to' question.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. It's what the author infers from Trollope ('few of the abandoned subplots'), and it may well be true. But the historian never assigns abandoned subplots to the writing side as opposed to the reading side; the passage says his term 'conflates' the two.
Too strong. Accepting a reader-side effect in Trollope doesn't commit the historian to dropping the writer side of his term. He still blames serial form for abandoned subplots too.

CORRECT. The historian's stated reason for counting Trollope (he wrote knowing readers would meet his work in parts) leaves only the readers' situation to explain the features. So the historian is committed to that situation producing them on its own. Note the hedge: 'some of the features.'
Contradicted. By the historian's own tally, Trollope's novels contain 'few' of these.
Nothing about relative skill. The historian's whole approach treats these features as responses to conditions, not as marks of talent.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Farm households in early New England lacked the cash to settle their accounts with neighbors, although they managed to settle promptly with merchants in distant towns.
Accounts between neighbors in early New England were closed exactly only when a death, a removal, or a lawsuit had already ended the relationship.
The open balances in New England households’ accounts, with neighbors and distant merchants alike, served chiefly to keep relationships between the parties alive.
The balances that neighbors left open in early New England accounts were most plausibly a deliberate means of keeping relationships of mutual aid alive.
Anthropological studies of gift exchange show that rural New England households valued their ties to neighbors more highly than any economic gain from trade.
questions.explanation: The passage sets out a puzzle (balances between neighbors carried forward for years), the earlier explanation (scarcity or careless bookkeeping), and a 'more persuasive explanation' (the open balance sustained relationships), then supports it. D states that favored explanation, with the author's hedge. C is the near-miss: it states the right mechanism but extends it to merchant accounts, which the passage says were settled 'promptly and to the penny.' B overstates the evidence ('only'), and A combines the rejected explanation with a detail.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage's central claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the puzzle and the old explanation); paragraph 2, first sentence ('A more persuasive explanation').

breakdown.analysis: What's the passage built around? A puzzle, an old answer, and a better answer that the author endorses ('more persuasive'). The rest is evidence for the better answer. So the main point is the better answer itself: the open balances were deliberate, a way of keeping neighbors bound to each other. Watch scope: the open balances were between neighbors only.

choices.note: Mixes the rejected explanation (lack of cash) with a detail from the evidence. And the author's point is that scarcity can't explain the pattern.
Tempting, because it's close to paragraph 3's last piece of evidence. But the records 'frequently' note a breach; the passage doesn't say accounts closed 'only' then.
Tempting: the mechanism is right. But the scope is wrong. Merchant accounts were closed 'promptly and to the penny'; the open balances were a neighbor phenomenon.

CORRECT. 'Deliberate means of keeping relationships of mutual aid alive' is the author's 'more persuasive explanation' (the balance was 'left outstanding by design' among households that relied on one another at harvest and in sickness). 'Most plausibly' matches the author's measured confidence.
Way too broad. The anthropological studies suggested the explanation; nothing says they prove anything about New England, let alone ranking ties over 'any' gain.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the households’ dealings with merchants in distant market towns?
choices: They were conducted largely in cash, which the households seldom had available for their dealings with neighbors.
They show that the households could close an account exactly when they chose to.
They mattered more to the households’ livelihood than did the exchanges the households recorded with neighbors.
They were reckoned at intervals roughly as long as those at which accounts with neighbors were reckoned.
They were frequently the occasion of the lawsuits noted in the town and court records of the period.
questions.explanation: The author cites the merchant accounts, settled 'promptly and to the penny' (third paragraph), as support for the view that the open balances with neighbors were deliberate; the contrast tells against both careless bookkeeping and an inability to settle. So the author takes these dealings to show that the households could close an account exactly when they chose, which is B. A is the attractive trap: it revives the scarcity explanation, which the author says 'cannot explain why the same households treated neighbors and merchants so differently.' E borrows the lawsuits from the same paragraph, where they concern neighbors' accounts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what the merchant accounts mean for the author's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence; paragraph 4, last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Why does the author bring up merchants at all? Because the same households, same bookkeepers, same shortage of cash, closed those accounts exactly. That knocks out 'too casual' and 'couldn't settle.' So the merchant accounts show the households could close accounts when they wanted to. The trap tries to explain the difference with cash, the very explanation the author rejects.

choices.note: Tempting, because it would explain the difference. But the passage never says how merchants were paid, and the author's point is that scarcity 'cannot explain' the difference. This reasoning is the earlier historians' side.
CORRECT. Prompt, to-the-penny settlement with merchants shows exact closing was within the households' power. That's what makes the open neighbor balances look chosen.
Not supported. The passage says nothing about which dealings mattered more economically.
Contradicted. Merchant accounts were settled 'promptly'; neighbor accounts were reckoned at 'long intervals.'
Tempting because lawsuits and court records are in the same paragraph, but they're tied to exactly closed accounts between neighbors.

questions.stem: By “a standing invitation” (last sentence of the second paragraph), the author most probably means
choices: a debt that remained legally enforceable for as long as the account between two households stayed open
an offer of hospitality that one household customarily extended to another whenever their accounts were reckoned
a balance left unpaid for so long that the household owed it no longer expected to be repaid
an ongoing signal that each household expected to go on exchanging goods and labor with the other
a request by the indebted household that its neighbor extend it another loan before the next reckoning
questions.explanation: The phrase sums up the explanation the author favors that a small remainder 'kept the expectation of future exchange alive' (second paragraph); D paraphrases that. A trades on the legal sense of 'standing,' and B on the literal sense of 'invitation'; the passage uses neither.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the metaphor in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Read the clause before it: the remainder 'kept the expectation of future exchange alive.' So the 'invitation' is to keep dealing, and it's 'standing' because it stays open. Ignore dictionary senses of the words.

choices.note: Uses the legal sense of 'standing.' The passage says nothing about enforceability; it calls the remainder 'less a debt' than an invitation.
Takes 'invitation' literally. The passage isn't about hospitality.
Opposite spirit. The point is that both sides expected the relationship to continue, not that one gave up.
CORRECT. 'Standing' = continuing; 'invitation' = to go on dealing with each other. Matches 'kept the expectation of future exchange alive.'
Nothing about requesting a new loan. The invitation is for exchange in general, mutual, not a debtor's request.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that both explanations offered by the earlier economic historians presuppose that
choices: the households kept their accounts with distant merchants as casually as they kept their accounts with their neighbors
an account closed with nothing owed on either side signaled the end of a relationship between two households
the open balances between neighbors were not something the households had set out to maintain
the balances carried forward between neighbors were too small to have mattered to the households
households in rural New England had little need of one another’s labor at harvest or in sickness
questions.explanation: The earlier historians explained the open balances either by scarcity ('farmers postponed settlement until they had cash') or by bookkeeping 'too casual to be brought to a close' (first paragraph). Each treats the open balance as an unintended result, a lapse, which presupposes C. The author's alternative is precisely that the balance was 'not a failure of settlement but its purpose' and 'left outstanding by design.' B is the author's view, the very premise the earlier explanations lack; A is not needed by either explanation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the earlier explanations both take for granted.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence; contrast paragraph 2 ('not a failure of settlement but its purpose'; 'by design').

breakdown.analysis: Two old explanations: no cash, or sloppy books. What do they share? Both make the open balance an accident, something that happened to the households rather than something they did on purpose. That's the assumption the author attacks with 'by design.' Prephrase: the balances weren't intended.

choices.note: Not presupposed. Neither explanation depends on how merchant accounts were kept. That contrast is the author's evidence against them.
This is the author's view, the one the earlier historians didn't hold.
CORRECT. Scarcity and careless bookkeeping both make the open balance an unintended lapse. The author's whole move is to say it was 'by design.'
Nothing in either explanation depends on the size of the balances.
Neither explanation needs this. They're about cash and bookkeeping, not how much neighbors relied on each other.

questions.stem: The passage cites each of the following as evidence for the explanation of the open balances that the author favors EXCEPT:
choices: the long intervals, sometimes of several years, at which accounts between neighbors were reckoned
the way the advantage in an account between two neighbors passed back and forth between them over the years
records connecting the exact closing of a neighbors’ account with a rupture of some kind between the two households
the exactness and speed with which the same households paid what they owed to merchants in market towns
the modest size of the amounts that neighbors left outstanding in their accounts with one another
questions.explanation: B through E paraphrase, in a different order, the four pieces of evidence in the third paragraph: the swinging balance, the deaths, removals, and lawsuits around exact closings, the prompt settlement with merchants, and the small remainders. A is an accurate detail, but the passage presents it in the first paragraph as part of the puzzle to be explained, not as evidence for the explanation. Because A sounds like the kind of fact that would fit the relationship explanation, test-takers who check only whether a choice is in the passage, or whether it seems consistent with the author's view, will miss it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one choice the passage does not use as evidence for its preferred explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (the evidence); paragraph 1 (the puzzle).

breakdown.analysis: All five choices are true to the passage, and all five sound friendly to the author's explanation. So neither 'is it mentioned?' nor 'does it fit?' sorts them. Ask what job each detail does. Paragraph 3 lists the evidence: merchant contrast, small remainders, swinging balance, closures with breaches. The long intervals belong to paragraph 1, where they describe what needs explaining.

choices.note: CORRECT. True, but it's part of the puzzle laid out in paragraph 1. The thing to be explained isn't cited as evidence for the explanation.
Cited. 'Over the years the balance tended to swing back and forth, so that each household was in turn creditor and debtor.'
Cited. Last sentence of paragraph 3: exact closings coincide with 'a death, a removal from the town, or a lawsuit,' each a break in the relationship.
Cited. Paragraph 3, second sentence: the same households settled with distant merchants 'promptly and to the penny.'
Cited. 'The remainders carried between neighbors were small.'

questions.stem: The author discusses the account that begins in the spring of 1792 primarily in order to
choices: demonstrate that the households in these towns settled with neighbors less exactly than they settled with merchants
illustrate the kind of careless bookkeeping that earlier economic historians attributed to farm households in rural New England
trace in one case how a neighbors’ balance alternated over many years and how it finally ended
suggest that the author’s explanation applies more clearly to loans of grain than to exchanges of labor
establish that disputes over boundaries were the most common reason that accounts between neighbors were closed
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens 'One account from these towns shows the pattern at work' and follows a single account through its alternations to its closing in a court quarrel; C describes that. A is the near-miss: the passage does make the neighbor/merchant contrast, but in the third paragraph; the 1792 account involves no merchant. E generalizes one case.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain the role of the 1792 example.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first sentence ('shows the pattern at work') and the rest of the paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The first sentence of the paragraph tells you the job: 'shows the pattern at work.' Which pattern? The swinging balance and the closure at a breach, from paragraph 3. So: one case that illustrates the general evidence.

choices.note: Tempting, because the contrast is part of the author's evidence. But the example contains no merchant account, so it can't show that comparison.
Opposite. The book records values carefully ('slightly more than a bushel'); the example supports the author, not the casual-bookkeeping view.
CORRECT. One account, followed through its swings and its closing in 1823 when the families went to court.
The example mixes grain and labor on purpose; nothing suggests the theory fits one better.
One case can't establish what's 'most common.'

questions.stem: If the author’s explanation of the open balances is correct, which one of the following was most likely true of a household new to the hill towns?
choices: To show good faith as a newcomer, it would have taken care to repay each neighbor exactly what it had borrowed.
It would have avoided borrowing from its neighbors until it had first established accounts with merchants in market towns.
To form lasting ties with a neighbor, it would have repaid that neighbor slightly more or slightly less than it had borrowed.
To demonstrate its commitment to a neighbor, it would have allowed a large balance to remain outstanding for many years.
It would have settled its accounts with distant merchants as slowly as it settled its accounts with its neighbors.
questions.explanation: On the author's explanation an exactly closed account signals that the relationship is over, while a small remainder keeps it open (second paragraph); a newcomer wishing to build ties would therefore leave small imbalances, as C says. A is the attractive misapplication: exact repayment looks like good faith, but on that explanation it would announce that the newcomer wanted no further dealings. D gets the mechanism but not the scale; the remainders were 'small.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's preferred explanation to a new case: a newcomer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (an exact close ends the relationship; a small remainder keeps it open); paragraph 3 (remainders were small).

breakdown.analysis: What does a newcomer want? Ties with neighbors. On the author's explanation, how do you get and keep ties? Leave a small balance open. Exact repayment sends the opposite message. So the newcomer should under- or over-pay a little. The trap is the common-sense answer that ignores the theory.

choices.note: Tempting, because in our world paying exactly shows you're trustworthy. But on the author's explanation, exact repayment says 'we're done.' Exactly wrong for someone who wants ties.
Nothing in the theory makes merchants a precondition for dealing with neighbors.
CORRECT. A small imbalance keeps the account, and the relationship, open. That's the mechanism applied to a newcomer.
Right idea, wrong size. The remainders were 'small'; nothing suggests large debts signaled commitment.
Opposite of the pattern. The same households settled with merchants promptly.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the explanation of the open balances that the author favors?
choices: Households in a neighboring region during the same period kept accounts with their own neighbors that nearly always balanced exactly.
Merchants in distant towns, unlike neighbors, refused further credit to any customer who had not paid off an earlier balance in full.
Cash was even scarcer in the hill towns during the period the studies cover than the earlier economic historians had supposed.
Some pairs of households that eventually sued each other had, in the years before the suit, kept accounts with balances that alternated.
Households that kept account books tended to be somewhat wealthier than households in the same towns that kept no books.
questions.explanation: The author's case rests heavily on the merchant contrast and on the claim that scarcity 'cannot explain why the same households treated neighbors and merchants so differently' (fourth paragraph). B supplies exactly such an explanation: households short of cash would spend it where full payment was a condition of further credit and let tolerant neighbors wait. That restores the scarcity account and removes the contrast's force. C is the dominant trap: it sounds like support for scarcity, but the author already concedes that cash was scarce; more scarcity does nothing to explain the difference in treatment. D fits the author's pattern, and A concerns another region.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines the claim that open balances were deliberate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence (the merchant contrast); paragraph 4, last three sentences (the concession about cash and the rebuttal).

breakdown.analysis: Where is the author's argument most exposed? At the rebuttal: 'cash was scarce, but scarcity can't explain why they treated neighbors and merchants differently.' So the strongest attack gives scarcity a way to explain that difference. If merchants cut off anyone who didn't pay in full, a cash-poor household pays the merchant first and lets the neighbor wait. Now the contrast is just triage, not a sign of intention. Most students pick (C) because it piles on scarcity. It fails because the author already grants scarcity; the question is the difference, and (C) says nothing about it.

choices.note: Another region isn't the hill towns. Different habits elsewhere tell us nothing about these households' intentions; if anything, the contrast fits a local custom.
CORRECT. It gives scarcity a way to produce the very neighbor/merchant difference the author says scarcity can't explain. The author's strongest evidence then fits the old explanation.
Tempting. This is the trap. The author already concedes cash 'was not' plentiful. More scarcity still doesn't explain why merchants were paid in full and neighbors weren't.
Fits the author's pattern: balances alternate while the relationship lasts, and the account closes with a breakdown.
So? Wealth differences between bookkeepers and non-bookkeepers don't explain why balances between neighbors stayed open.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?
choices: Can the adversarial method adequately test the conclusions that expert witnesses present at trial?
How can experts retained by the parties be made less partisan in the testimony they give at trial?
Should courts make use of their power to appoint expert witnesses of their own choosing?
What procedures should courts follow in selecting the experts whom they appoint in technical disputes?
Are jurors capable of choosing rationally between the conflicting conclusions of two partisan experts?
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that judges are right to be reluctant to appoint their own experts, and passage B argues for appointing them; both are centrally about whether courts should use the power, which is C. A is the closest trap: both passages touch on how well adversarial procedure tests expert testimony, but only as support for their positions on appointment. D is a concern of passage B's third paragraph only, E of passage B's first paragraph only, and B is touched only by passage A's closing remedy.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one question that both passages are mainly trying to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 1 ('sound reasons for the reluctance') and paragraph 4 (the alternative remedy); passage B, paragraph 2 (the case for a court-appointed expert).

breakdown.analysis: A says: don't use the power, here's why. B says: use it, here's why and how. Same question, opposite answers: should courts appoint their own experts? Every 'both' answer must be central to A and to B. Watch for questions only one passage takes up.

choices.note: Tempting, because both passages touch it: A's last paragraph wants to strengthen adversarial testing, and B's first paragraph describes clashing partisan experts. But in each it's a supporting point. Neither passage is mainly about it; the question both take sides on is whether courts should appoint their own experts.
Only passage A's last sentence gestures at improving adversarial testing, and it doesn't try to make party experts less partisan. B accepts party experts as partisan and looks elsewhere.
CORRECT. A answers no, B answers yes. That's the shared question.
Selection procedures are passage B's third paragraph only. A raises selection as a problem, not as a procedure to design.
Passage B's first paragraph worries about this. Passage A never addresses jurors' ability to choose between party experts.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage A but not in passage B?
choices: the possibility that a judge could ask a professional body to propose candidates for appointment
the reluctance of attorneys to cross-examine forcefully an expert witness whom the judge has chosen
the existence of technical fields in which competent specialists disagree with one another
the tendency of jurors to credit whichever of two experts seems more poised and likable
the right of parties to present their own experts even when the court has appointed one
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph of passage A says a lawyer who sharply cross-examines the judge's witness 'risks appearing to quarrel with the judge, and few lawyers will run that risk'; passage B says only that parties 'remain free' to cross-examine the court's expert, which is about permission, not reluctance, so B is correct. C is the likeliest trap, but it appears in both passages (A's 'competent specialists disagree,' third paragraph; B's 'Where a field is genuinely divided,' third paragraph). A, D, and E appear only in passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the item that passage A mentions and passage B does not.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 4 (lawyers' reluctance to cross-examine the court's expert) and paragraph 3 (divided fields); passage B, paragraphs 1-3.

breakdown.analysis: Two checks per choice: is it in A? Is it absent from B? Lawyers being reluctant to go hard at the judge's own witness is A's third objection (its fourth paragraph). B mentions cross-examining the court's expert only to say the parties 'remain free' to do it. Free to do it isn't the same as reluctant to do it.

choices.note: Only in passage B (third paragraph: 'ask a professional body to propose a panel').
CORRECT. Passage A's fourth paragraph: 'few lawyers will run that risk.' B talks only about the parties' freedom to cross-examine, not any reluctance.
Tempting, because it's prominent in A's 'Second' paragraph. But B mentions it too: 'Where a field is genuinely divided.' In both, so it fails.
Only in passage B (first paragraph, the mock-juror studies).
Only in passage B (second paragraph: 'The parties remain free to call their own witnesses').

questions.stem: Passage B suggests which one of the following about experts retained by litigants?
choices: They are generally less competent in their fields than the experts whom a court would appoint.
They tend to seem less poised and likable to jurors than do experts appointed by the court.
They should not be permitted to testify in cases in which the court has appointed an expert of its own.
They seldom reach conflicting conclusions except in fields in which the science is genuinely unsettled.
Their value to the party that retains them need not depend on how sound their views actually are.
questions.explanation: Passage B says litigants retain the expert whose views serve their case or 'for an adequate fee, can be made to serve it,' and that jurors tend to credit whichever expert seems more poised and likable, 'a standard unrelated to the merits' (first paragraph). So an expert can be useful to a party for reasons other than soundness, which is E. A is the near-miss: passage B says the court's expert is chosen 'for competence rather than for persuasiveness,' which concerns how each is selected, not whether party experts are less competent. C contradicts passage B's statement that parties 'remain free to call their own witnesses.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage B implies about the parties' own experts.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 1 (selection by litigants; jurors' 'standard unrelated to the merits') and paragraph 2 ('chosen for competence rather than for persuasiveness').

breakdown.analysis: Why do litigants pick the experts they pick? Because their views serve the case, or can be made to for a fee. And what wins with jurors? Poise and likability, 'unrelated to the merits.' Put together: what makes an expert valuable to a party isn't necessarily being right. The key says this abstractly, so it may not look like the answer at first. Watch the trap that turns 'chosen for persuasiveness' into 'less competent': a hired gun can be brilliant.

choices.note: Tempting, because passage B contrasts an expert 'chosen for competence' with one chosen for persuasiveness. But that's about the basis of selection. A persuasive expert can also be highly competent; B never says otherwise.
Not supported. The mock-juror studies say jurors credit whichever of the two party experts seems more poised, not that party experts seem less poised than court experts.
Contradicted. Passage B: 'The parties remain free to call their own witnesses.'
Passage B never says when party experts agree. It says that in technical disputes they often produce 'irreconcilable' conclusions.

CORRECT. Experts are picked because their views serve the case (or can be made to), and they win jurors over on poise, not merit. So their value to the party needn't track soundness. 'Need not' is the right strength.

questions.stem: The relationship between passage A and passage B is most analogous to the relationship between the documents described in which one of the following?
choices: an essay titled “Neutral in Name Only: The Case Against Arbitrator-Appointed Appraisers” and an essay titled “Sharpening the Contest: Earlier Exchange of Rival Appraisal Reports”
an essay titled “A Fixed Point Among Valuations: In Defense of Tribunal Appraisers” and an essay titled “The Unseen Partisanship of Tribunal-Appointed Appraisers”
an essay titled “The Unreliability of Appraisers Hired by the Parties” and an essay titled “Choosing a Tribunal’s Appraiser: Nomination, Panels, and Consent”
an essay titled “Appraisal in Arbitration: A Brief History” and an essay titled “Between Two Hired Valuations: Why Arbitrators Need an Appraiser of Their Own”
an essay titled “Why Arbitrators Should Hesitate to Choose Their Own Appraisers” and an essay titled “Measuring the Hired Experts: The Case for a Tribunal’s Own Appraiser”
questions.explanation: Passage A argues against a decision maker's appointing its own supposedly neutral expert, and passage B defends that practice as giving decision makers a fixed point against which to measure rival partisan experts (second paragraph of passage B); E reproduces both stances, in order, including B's measuring rationale. A is the closest trap: its first title fits passage A, and its second echoes passage A's own closing remedy, but neither essay defends the decision maker's expert. B reverses the order, C pairs two pro-appointment essays (one on selection procedure, which is only passage B's third paragraph), and D opens with a neutral history.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the pair of titles whose relationship mirrors A (against court-chosen experts) then B (for them).

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 1 (the stance) and paragraph 4 (its remedy); passage B, paragraph 2 ('a fixed point against which to measure them') and paragraph 3 (selection procedures).

breakdown.analysis: Strip out the courtroom: essay 1 argues against a decision maker choosing its own 'neutral' expert; essay 2 defends it as a yardstick for measuring two hired guns. Order matters: critique first, defense second. No pair shares a title with the key, so you have to judge each title's stance yourself. Check each pair for both halves and for the order.

choices.note: Tempting. The first title fits passage A, and the second matches passage A's own remedy ('earlier disclosure of expert reports'). But that's two essays on A's side. Nothing defends the arbitrator's appraiser.
Right two stances, wrong order. Defense first, critique second is B-then-A.
Both titles are on passage B's side: the first is B's complaint about party experts, the second B's third paragraph on selection. No critique of the tribunal's appraiser comes first.
The second title fits passage B, but the first is a neutral history, and passage A is a critique.
CORRECT. A case against the decision maker choosing its own appraiser, then a defense built on 'measuring the hired experts,' which is B's 'fixed point against which to measure them.'

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: jurors’ readiness to defer to an expert chosen by the court counts against the practice of appointing one
jurors are likely to give a court-appointed expert’s testimony more weight than they give the testimony of either party’s expert
parties should be permitted to cross-examine an expert whom the court itself has appointed
the testimony of experts retained by litigants tends to reflect the interests of the litigants who retained them
competent specialists in some technical fields sometimes reach conflicting conclusions on questions that come before a court
questions.explanation: Passage A's first objection (second paragraph) is that jurors will treat the court's expert's opinion 'as a verdict to be ratified'; passage B replies (second paragraph) that if jurors give that expert more weight, 'that is hardly a defect.' So they disagree over whether jurors' deference counts against appointment, which is A. B is the dominant trap: passage A asserts that jurors will give the court's expert more weight, but passage B never denies it; its 'if' clause leaves the point open. D and E are views both authors hold, and C is something passage A never addresses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would accept and the other would reject. Both authors must take a side.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A paragraph 2 (jurors treat the court's expert's opinion 'as a verdict to be ratified'); passage B paragraph 2 ('if jurors give the court's expert more weight ... that is hardly a defect').

breakdown.analysis: Do the authors disagree about whether jurors defer to the court's expert, or about whether that deference is bad? Look at B's wording: 'if jurors give the court's expert more weight.' That's an 'if'. B never says they won't. So the disagreement isn't about the fact; it's about what the fact means. A says it's a reason against appointment. B says it's no defect. We need an answer about the significance of the deference. Most students pick (B) because it's the most obvious point of contrast. But to disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. Passage B never says no.

choices.note: CORRECT. A treats jurors' deference as a reason not to appoint (the expert 'effectively' decides the case). B says the extra weight is 'hardly a defect'. One yes, one no, on whether the deference counts against the practice.

Tempting. This is the trap. Passage A says yes. But passage B says only 'if jurors give the court's expert more weight', which is a conditional, not a denial. B has no stated view on whether they will, so there's no disagreement here.
Passage B says the parties remain free to cross-examine. Passage A never says they shouldn't be; it says lawyers are reluctant to do it hard. No disagreement.
Both agree. A calls for a remedy for 'partisan expertise'; B says litigants pick experts whose views serve their case.
Both agree. A says competent specialists disagree in unsettled fields; B's 'two confident witnesses whose conclusions are irreconcilable' and its 'range of respectable opinion' concede the same.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be likely to offer regarding the suggestion in the last sentence of passage B?
choices: Such an instruction would discourage jurors from giving the court’s expert the additional weight that the expert’s neutrality rightly warrants.
Such an instruction would not keep jurors who know that the judge chose the expert from treating that expert’s opinion as authoritative.
Such an instruction would reveal to jurors a fact about how the expert was selected that they would otherwise never learn.
Such an instruction would make attorneys more willing to cross-examine the court’s expert aggressively, needlessly prolonging technical trials.
Such an instruction would be unnecessary, since jurors already regard the court’s expert as no more reliable than other witnesses.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of passage B proposes telling jurors that the court's expert can be mistaken and that they remain free to reject her testimony. Passage A's first objection (second paragraph) is that jurors told a witness was chosen by the judge treat that witness's opinion 'not as evidence to be weighed but as a verdict to be ratified'; an instruction that leaves jurors knowing who chose the expert would not dispel that aura, so B is correct. A states passage B's view of the added weight, not passage A's. C is tempting because passage A says the jury 'is unlikely ever to learn' something, but that refers to the choice of doctrine (third paragraph). D and E conflict with passage A's own concerns.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how A's author would object to B's proposal that judges remind jurors that the court's expert can be mistaken and may be rejected.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, paragraph 3, last sentence (the jury instruction); passage A, paragraph 2 (jurors treat the court's witness as authoritative).

breakdown.analysis: First find the suggestion: the last sentence of B, a jury instruction that the court's expert can be wrong and that jurors may reject her testimony. Now think like A. A's first worry is that jurors who know the judge picked the expert defer to that expert. Would a sentence from the judge undo that? A would doubt it: the jurors still know who chose the witness. Prephrase: the instruction won't stop the deference.

choices.note: That's B's view (the court's expert 'deserves more weight'), not A's. A thinks the extra weight is the problem.
CORRECT. A's second paragraph says knowing the judge chose the witness turns opinion into 'a verdict to be ratified.' An instruction doesn't erase that knowledge.

Tempting, because A says the jury 'is unlikely ever to learn' something. But that's about the hidden choice of doctrine in a divided field (A's third paragraph), not about who selected the expert. Jurors already know that.
Backward. A worries lawyers won't cross-examine the court's expert; it wouldn't complain that they'd do it more.
Contradicts A, which says jurors see the court's expert as more neutral than any party's expert.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes how passage B responds to the concern raised in the second paragraph of passage A?
choices: It leaves open whether jurors would give the court’s expert added weight and maintains that, if they did, this would not be objectionable.
It denies that jurors give a court-appointed expert more weight than the parties’ own experts, citing studies in which mock jurors credited whichever expert was more likable.
It concedes that jurors would give the court’s expert added weight but argues that the benefits of appointing an expert outweigh that cost.
It maintains that a suitable instruction would keep jurors from giving the court’s expert any more weight than they give the parties’ experts.
It dismisses the concern as speculative on the grounds that the court’s expert, like any other witness, can be cross-examined by either party.
questions.explanation: Passage A's second paragraph worries that jurors will treat the court's expert's opinion as 'a verdict to be ratified.' Passage B answers conditionally: 'if jurors give the court's expert more weight than either party's, that is hardly a defect,' since an expert chosen for competence 'deserves more weight' (second paragraph). It neither affirms nor denies the factual claim and rejects the claim that the extra weight is bad, which is A. C is the near-miss: it treats the extra weight as a cost to be outweighed, but B denies that it is a defect at all. D misreads B's closing jury instruction, which only reminds jurors that the expert can be mistaken; it does not aim to equalize weight that B says the expert deserves.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize passage B's answer to A's worry that jurors will defer to the court's expert.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2; passage B, paragraph 2 ('if jurors give... that is hardly a defect') and paragraph 3, last sentence (the jury instruction).

breakdown.analysis: Read B's sentence slowly: 'if jurors give the court's expert more weight..., that is hardly a defect.' Two moves. The 'if' means B doesn't commit on whether jurors will do it. 'Hardly a defect' means B rejects the evaluation, not the fact. So B's reply is about the significance, not the occurrence. The traps each misdescribe one of those moves: one has B deny the fact, one has B admit a cost, and one reads the jury instruction as an effort to equalize weight.

choices.note: CORRECT. The 'if' leaves the factual question open; 'hardly a defect' says the extra weight wouldn't be objectionable. That's the whole response.
The mock-juror studies are in passage B, but they concern jurors choosing between two party experts. B never denies that the court's expert gets more weight.
Tempting. It sounds like a balanced reading. But B doesn't call the extra weight a cost; it says the weight is deserved and 'hardly a defect.' Nothing is being outweighed.

Wrong job for the instruction. B's closing instruction only tells jurors that the court's expert 'can be mistaken' and that they may reject her testimony. It says nothing about matching the weight given the parties' experts, and B has just said the court's expert 'deserves more weight.'
B mentions that parties can cross-examine the court's expert, but never calls A's concern speculative. It answers the concern on its merits.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that dams and weirs that block salmon runs are the principal cause of the pearl mussel’s failure to reproduce
describe a method of aging long-lived animals and show how it overturned an earlier estimate of a species’ abundance
argue that field observations have established which of two proposed causes accounts for a species’ reproductive failure
account for the late discovery of a species’ reproductive failure and weigh the evidence on two explanations of it
criticize conservation programs that rear young mussels in captivity for failing to address the causes of decline
questions.explanation: The passage explains why counts of long-lived adults hid the failure to reproduce (first paragraph), lays out the life cycle and two explanations (second and third paragraphs), weighs field evidence that points toward the riverbed but is not decisive (fourth paragraph), and notes that the two explanations call for different remedies (fifth paragraph). D covers this. C is the near-miss: the evidence does 'point toward the riverbed,' but the author says it bears on the question 'less decisively than is sometimes claimed.' B misdescribes the first paragraph, which says nothing about an earlier estimate being overturned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the passage as a whole sets out to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the hidden failure); paragraph 3 (two explanations); paragraph 4 (evidence, 'less decisively than is sometimes claimed'); paragraph 5 (why it matters).

breakdown.analysis: Does the author ever pick a winner? Map it: hidden failure (P1), life cycle (P2), two explanations and why age data can't decide (P3), evidence that leans toward sediment plus two caveats (P4), why the answer matters (P5). The author leans, then pulls back: 'less decisively than is sometimes claimed.' So the purpose is to explain the late discovery and weigh evidence on the two explanations, not to declare one proven.

choices.note: Too strong, and it picks the host-fish explanation, which the author never names as principal.
Aging by growth lines is one sentence of P1, and the passage describes a population counted as 'diminished but stable,' not an overturned estimate.

Tempting, because both findings in P4 'point toward the riverbed.' But the author says they bear on the question 'less decisively than is sometimes claimed' and then gives two reasons for caution. Nothing is established.
CORRECT. 'Late discovery' = P1 (adults counted as stable until shells were aged); 'two explanations' = P3; 'weigh the evidence' = P4's findings and caveats.
Captive rearing gets one sentence in P5, which says the programs 'buy time.' That's a limit noted in passing, not the passage's purpose.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Surveys that simply count the mussels in a river tend to overstate the number of adult mussels living there.
The sediment explanation accounts for the missing generations in more rivers than the host-fish explanation does.
Programs that rear juveniles in captivity should be abandoned in favor of measures that restore the riverbed.
A finding that a river’s host fish carry glochidia in abundance would not by itself show that its mussels are secure.
The age structure of a river’s mussel population can reveal which of the two stresses caused its reproductive failure.
questions.explanation: The author reports rivers where trout carry glochidia 'in abundance, yet no young mussels are found in the gravel' (fourth paragraph), so abundant infestation alone would not show a population is secure, which is D. A is tempting because the first paragraph faults surveys that 'simply count mussels,' but the fault is that an accurate count of adults hides the failure to reproduce, not that it inflates the number of adults. B overstates evidence the author calls not decisive, C contradicts 'buy time,' and E contradicts the third paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer a view the author holds, drawing on more than one paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (what simple counts miss); paragraph 4 (trout with glochidia but no young mussels; the caveats); paragraph 5 ('buy time').

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test each choice against the text. The author's big themes: counts of adults mislead about reproduction; failure can occur at the host stage or in the gravel.
