Combine them: even if the host stage looks healthy, the gravel can still kill every juvenile, so a healthy-looking host stage doesn't prove the population is safe. Watch the trap that over-reads paragraph 1: the counts weren't wrong about how many adults there were; they were silent about the young.

choices.note: Tempting, because paragraph 1 criticizes surveys that 'simply count mussels.' But the problem is what an accurate count hides (no young animals), not an inflated number of adults. Nothing suggests the counts were too high.
Overreach. The author says the field evidence bears on the question 'less decisively than is sometimes claimed' and gives no count of rivers.
Too strong. The author says such programs 'buy time,' which is a mild endorsement, not a call to abandon them.

CORRECT. Paragraph 4 describes rivers where trout carry glochidia in abundance and still no young mussels survive. So abundant infestation alone can't show a population is secure. 'By itself' is the needed qualifier.
Contradicted. Paragraph 3 says the age structure 'cannot by itself decide between them.'

questions.stem: The author mentions trout examined in late summer that carry encysted glochidia in abundance (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: establish that the host-fish explanation cannot account for the missing generations in any of the rivers concerned
show that the glochidia encysted on those fish complete their development and drop off as juveniles
point to an observation suggesting that in certain rivers reproduction fails at some stage after larvae have found hosts
illustrate the process by which glochidia become attached to and encysted on the gills of young salmon and trout
show that host fish are no longer scarce in the rivers in which the mussel has ceased to reproduce
questions.explanation: The trout observation is one of two findings that 'point toward the riverbed' (fourth paragraph): the larvae have reached their hosts, yet no young mussels appear, so the breakdown seems to come after the host stage. C says this abstractly and keeps the author's hedge; even the caveat that a glochidium may be lost before it matures places the failure after larvae have found hosts. B is the near-miss: it turns the observation into proof of completed development, which is exactly what the caveat denies. E generalizes 'a number of rivers' to all rivers, and A overstates evidence the author calls not decisive.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the trout observation contributes to the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, sentences 1-2 and the caveat in the last sentence; paragraph 3 (the host explanation locates failure 'early in the cycle,' the sediment explanation 'later').

breakdown.analysis: Why would it matter that trout are full of glochidia? Because the host explanation says there aren't enough fish to carry them. If the larvae have found hosts and there are still no young mussels, the breakdown must come after that point. But read the caveat: a glochidium 'may still be lost from its host before it matures.' So the author doesn't claim the larvae made it to the gravel, only that they got onto fish. The right answer has to say exactly that much and no more.

choices.note: Too strong twice: the observation comes from 'a number of rivers,' and the author says the evidence is less decisive than sometimes claimed.

Tempting, because the observation seems to clear the host stage. But the author warns that an encysted glochidium 'may still be lost from its host before it matures.' The observation doesn't show completed development.

CORRECT. The larvae have found hosts, yet no young mussels appear, so in those rivers the failure comes somewhere after that point. 'Suggesting' matches the author's hedge, and the claim survives the caveat.
The process of attachment is described in paragraph 2. Here the trout serve as evidence, not as an illustration of the process.

Tempting, since abundant infestation implies hosts are present. But the observation concerns 'a number of rivers,' not every river where the mussel has stopped reproducing, and the host explanation remains live elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the support that the container experiments (fourth paragraph) give the sediment explanation?
choices: Juveniles reared in hatcheries are somewhat less hardy than juveniles of the same age that have developed in the wild.
In several streams in which the hatchery-reared juveniles survived well, no young wild mussels have been found in the gravel.
Fine sediment entering rivers from farmland increased over the same decades in which salmon and trout populations declined.
Juvenile pearl mussels remain buried in gravel for a larger portion of their lives than do juveniles of most other mussel species.
Juveniles held in containers suspended above the riverbed, out of contact with the gravel, survived poorly in exactly the same streams.
questions.explanation: The experiments support the sediment explanation because juvenile survival tracked the amount of fine material in the gravel. E shows that juveniles kept out of the gravel died in the same streams, so something in those streams' water, not the sediment in their beds, may be killing them. B is the dominant trap: it seems to cut against the sediment view, but the experiments show only that sediment can kill juveniles, and the absence of wild young where caged ones thrive is what a host shortage in those streams would produce; the author allows that a given river may suffer from either stress or both. A applies equally to every stream and so leaves the comparison intact, and C restates a fact the passage already grants.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that undercuts the inference from the caged-juvenile experiments to the sediment explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, third sentence (survival 'roughly in proportion to how much fine material fills the gravel'); paragraph 3 (the sediment explanation).

breakdown.analysis: What's the inference? Juveniles died where the gravel was full of fine material, so the fine material killed them. That's a correlation. How do you attack it? Show that something else differs between those streams and does the killing. The cleanest version: take the gravel out of the picture and see whether the deaths still follow the same streams. Most students pick (B) because it sounds like evidence against the sediment view. It fails because the experiment's claim is only that sediment kills juveniles where it's heavy; streams with clean gravel and no wild young are just streams where something else (like a shortage of hosts) is the problem, and the passage never treats the two explanations as exclusive.

choices.note: Tempting, but hatchery juveniles were used in every stream. If they're a bit less hardy, that lowers survival everywhere and leaves the stream-to-stream pattern, the actual evidence, untouched.

Tempting. This is the trap. It sounds like the sediment story failing. But the experiments say heavy sediment kills juveniles; they don't say clean gravel guarantees wild young. A clean stream with no young mussels could simply lack infested hosts.
Irrelevant corroboration. The passage already says both stresses intensified over the same decades. It doesn't touch the experiment.
So? How long juveniles stay buried doesn't affect whether survival differences came from sediment.

CORRECT. Same death pattern without contact with the gravel means something in the water of those streams, not the sediment in their beds, may explain the results. The correlation with fine material loses its force.

questions.stem: Which one of the following situations is most analogous to the situation of the pearl mussel populations described in the first paragraph?
choices: A town whose population has held steady for decades because the young people who move away are replaced by retirees who move there from elsewhere.
A forest in which most of the old trees have been felled but saplings are abundant, so that it looks depleted though it is regenerating.
A resort town whose population swells each summer with visitors, so that a census taken in summer overstates its permanent residents.
A professional society whose roster has barely shrunk in twenty years because members seldom leave, though its records show that almost no one has joined.
A herd that is culled every year to hold its size constant, so that annual counts show no change despite heavy yearly losses.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes populations that look 'diminished but stable' only because the adults live so long, masking the fact that no young are being added. D matches every element: long-lived members keep the count up while recruitment has stopped, a fact visible only in the records. A is the closest near-miss: its population also looks steady while aging, but it is being replenished by newcomers, so it has not ceased to replace itself. E's counts also conceal something, but its losses are offset by yearly replacement, and B reverses the relation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of the first paragraph's situation to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, second sentence ('diminished but stable long after it has ceased to replace itself').

breakdown.analysis: Strip out the biology: a group looks fairly steady because its members last a long time, but nobody new is joining, so it's actually dying. The analogy must have all three: long-lived members, a count that looks steady, and stopped replacement hidden by that count. Two choices have a steady count that hides something; only one has no replacement at all.

choices.note: Tempting: steady numbers, an aging population. But the town is being replenished, by retirees instead of children. The mussels aren't being replenished by anyone, which is why they will eventually collapse.
Reversed: this looks worse than it is. The mussels looked better than they were.
Counts mislead here, but because of temporary visitors, not long-lived members hiding a lack of new ones.

CORRECT. Members who seldom leave keep the roster full while almost no one joins, and only the records reveal it. The steady count hides a stopped renewal, just as growth lines revealed the missing young mussels.
Tempting: counts hide something. But the herd is being replaced every year (that's how its size holds). The mussels aren't being replaced at all.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following?
choices: In rivers where young salmon and trout are plentiful, pearl mussel populations can generally be expected to be reproducing successfully.
Programs that rear young pearl mussels in captivity have done nothing to slow the decline of the populations they are meant to help.
In most rivers where the pearl mussel survives, fine sediment rather than a shortage of host fish accounts for the absence of young mussels.
If either explanation is correct, most of the surviving adults were produced before the stress it identifies had become severe.
Removing the fine sediment from a river’s gravel would by itself be enough to restore reproduction in that river’s pearl mussels.
questions.explanation: The surviving animals are mostly several decades old (first paragraph), and both stresses 'intensified over the same decades in which recruitment ceased' (third paragraph). Each explanation holds that its stress is what stopped recruitment, so on either one the adults now present were produced before that stress became severe, which is D. E is the dominant trap: it follows the findings that 'point toward the riverbed' but ignores that the host-fish explanation is still live and that a river may suffer from both stresses. C overstates evidence the author calls not decisive, and A ignores rivers where trout carry glochidia yet no young mussels appear.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim that the passage's statements, taken together, most strongly support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (almost no animals younger than several decades); paragraph 3, last sentence (the stresses intensified as recruitment ceased); paragraphs 4-5 (evidence not decisive; a river may suffer from both).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so link the facts. 1. The mussels left are old. 2. Recruitment stopped decades ago. 3. Both stresses intensified in the very decades recruitment stopped. 4. Each explanation says its stress is what stopped it. So, on either explanation, when were today's adults born? Before that stress got bad. The key is conditional ('If either explanation is correct'), which makes it look weak or off-point, but that hedge is exactly what makes it safe. The tempting wrong answers take paragraph 4's lean toward sediment and run with it.

choices.note: Contradicted. Paragraph 4 describes rivers where trout carry glochidia in abundance, yet no young mussels are found.
Too strong. The author says such programs 'buy time,' which means they do slow the decline.
Overreach. The author says the field evidence bears on the question 'less decisively than is sometimes claimed.' No claim about most rivers.

CORRECT. Each explanation names a stress that stopped recruitment, and recruitment stopped as the stresses intensified. So whichever is right, the old adults predate the severe phase of that stress. The 'if' clause keeps the inference within what the passage supports.

Tempting. This is the trap: it follows the findings that 'point toward the riverbed.' But the host-fish explanation is still open, and 'a given river may, of course, suffer from both.' Clean gravel can't be shown to be enough by itself.

questions.stimulus: Coach: Our league should not adopt the proposed rule limiting youth pitchers to forty pitches per game. The rule's supporters say it will reduce arm injuries, and that is a worthy aim. But most arm injuries among our players occur during off-season travel tournaments, which the league does not govern. So a pitch limit in league games would do little to protect players' arms.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the coach's argument?
choices: Reducing arm injuries among the league's youth pitchers is a worthy aim that the rule's supporters share.
A limit on pitches in league games would do little to protect the arms of the league's young players.
Most arm injuries suffered by the league's players occur during off-season travel tournaments.
The league should begin to govern the off-season travel tournaments in which most arm injuries occur.
The league should not adopt the proposed rule limiting youth pitchers to forty pitches per game.
questions.explanation: The coach's point is the opening claim that the league should not adopt the pitch limit; everything else supports it, so E is correct. B is the trap: it is supported by the claim about travel tournaments, but it is offered as the reason for rejecting the rule, so it is an intermediate conclusion. C is a premise, A a concession, and D is never proposed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The league should not adopt the forty-pitch limit.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reducing arm injuries is worthy (concession); but most arm injuries happen in off-season travel tournaments the league doesn't govern; so a league pitch limit would do little to protect arms.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Here it comes first, which is common. The "So" sentence at the end looks like a conclusion, but ask why the coach says it: to explain why the league shouldn't adopt the rule. That makes it a stepping stone. Lesson: "so" doesn't always mark the main conclusion.

choices.note: A concession. The coach grants that the aim is worthy before arguing against the rule. Not the point being proved.
Tempting. It's flagged by "So" and it is supported by the tournament fact. But it's offered as the reason not to adopt the rule. Intermediate, not main.
A premise. It's the evidence that a league pitch limit wouldn't help much.
The coach never proposes this. Saying the league doesn't govern tournaments isn't saying it should.
CORRECT. The opening claim. The travel-tournament fact and the little protection the rule would give are both there to support it.

questions.stimulus: The city council can close next year's budget gap by raising property taxes, and it can also close the gap by reducing the public library's hours. But a majority of council members have publicly pledged not to raise property taxes this year, and none has shown any sign of breaking that pledge. So the council will have no choice but to reduce the library's hours.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that the budget gap might be closed by some means other than the two that it mentions
takes for granted that reducing the library's hours would be more popular with the city's residents than raising property taxes
confuses what the council is likely to do about the budget gap with what the council ought to do about it
treats the views of a majority of the council's members as representative of the views of the city's residents
infers that the council members will keep their pledge merely from the fact that they made it in public
questions.explanation: The premises say only that each of two measures could close the gap; they never say these are the only ways. Ruling out one measure therefore does not leave the council with 'no choice' but the other. A names this. E is tempting but misdescribes the argument, which backs the pledge with the members' conduct, and in any case the pledge is a premise the argument may use. B, C, and D describe reasoning about popularity, obligation, and representativeness that the argument never engages in.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council will have no choice but to reduce the library's hours.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Raising property taxes would close the gap; cutting library hours would also close it; most council members have pledged not to raise taxes.

breakdown.analysis: No choice? Says who? The premises tell us two things that WOULD close the gap. They never say those are the only two. The council could cut another department, sell property, or raise a fee. That's a false choice: treat two options as the only options, knock one out, and declare the other inevitable. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the argument ignores other ways to close the gap.

choices.note: CORRECT. Two ways to close the gap were mentioned, not two ways only. Rule out taxes and other options are still open, so "no choice" doesn't follow.
Popularity never comes up. The argument says the council has no choice, not that residents prefer library cuts.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We should cut library hours, since surely people care less about the library than about their taxes.

choices.note: The conclusion is about what the council will be forced to do, not what it should do. There's no slide from 'likely' to 'ought.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The council will probably cut library hours, so cutting them is the right thing to do.

choices.note: The argument never draws a conclusion about residents' views, so it can't be treating the council as a sample of them.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most council members oppose tax hikes, so most residents must oppose them too.

choices.note: Tempting, because the pledge is the shakiest-sounding fact. But the argument doesn't rest on the pledge alone; it adds that no member has shown any sign of breaking it. And even granting the pledge holds, the real gap remains: taxes and library hours aren't the only two options.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The mayor said in public that she won't close the pool, so the pool will certainly stay open.

questions.stimulus: Striped grunters, a reef fish common around the Caribbean island of Corva, feed mostly at night, which is when they are most active. Yet in the island's annual reef census, conducted each spring by volunteers, divers who survey the reef during the day consistently count far more striped grunters than do divers who survey the same stretches of reef at night.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why divers count more striped grunters by day than by night?
choices: At night striped grunters leave the reef to feed in distant seagrass beds, returning to rest over the reef by day.
Several species of eels that prey on striped grunters hunt over the reef mainly at night, when the grunters are active.
Divers who survey the reef at night carry powerful lights that make fish visible from a considerable distance.
The striped grunter is among the most numerous of all the fish species that live on the island's reef.
Many of the other fish species found in the waters near the island also do most of their feeding at night.
questions.explanation: You would expect a fish active at night to be easier to find at night. A explains the pattern: the grunters feed away from the reef at night and are over the reef, where divers survey, by day. C deepens the puzzle, B does not explain why the fish would be seen more often by day, and D and E do not distinguish day from night counts.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Striped grunters are most active at night, but divers count far more of them on the reef by day.

breakdown.analysis: Why would an active fish be harder to find? Activity isn't the same as being where the divers look. We need an answer that puts the grunters somewhere other than the surveyed reef at night, or makes them harder to see then.

choices.note: CORRECT. Divers survey the reef. At night the grunters are off in the seagrass beds; by day they're resting right over the reef. So more are counted by day.
Predators hunting at night might make grunters hide, but the answer doesn't say that. Eels hunting at night don't by themselves explain why divers see fewer grunters on the reef.
Wrong direction. Powerful lights should make night counts higher, which deepens the puzzle.
Interesting fact, but it applies day and night alike. Abundance can't explain a difference between the two.
So? Other species' habits say nothing about why grunter counts differ between day and night.

questions.stimulus:
Rosa: The Marlton city orchestra should devote nearly all of its programs to established classical works. Those works draw the largest audiences, and ticket sales are what keep the orchestra solvent.

Malik: Ticket sales certainly matter. But an orchestra that plays only familiar works will gradually lose younger listeners, who are its future audience. The orchestra should give a substantial share of its programs to new compositions.
questions.stem: Rosa and Malik disagree over whether
choices: younger listeners generally prefer new compositions to the established classical works the orchestra now plays
established classical works draw larger audiences than new compositions do at the orchestra's concerts
only a small part of the orchestra's programs should go to anything other than established classics
ticket sales are important to the overall financial health of the Marlton city orchestra
attracting younger listeners today is important to the long-term financial health of the Marlton city orchestra
questions.explanation: Rosa says nearly all programs should be established works; Malik says a substantial share should go to new compositions, so he rejects leaving only a small part for anything else. They disagree about C, which restates Rosa's 'nearly all' from the other side. Malik concedes that ticket sales matter (D) and never disputes that classics draw larger audiences (B). Rosa says nothing about younger listeners, so she takes no side on A or E, though Malik's view implies E.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Rosa: nearly all programs should be established classics, because they draw the biggest audiences and ticket sales keep the orchestra solvent; Malik: ticket sales matter, but playing only familiar works loses younger listeners, so a substantial share of programs should be new works.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Rosa's yes: nearly all programs should be classics. Malik's no: a substantial share should be new compositions, which can't happen if nearly all are classics. The right answer says this in different words: 'only a small part' for non-classics is just 'nearly all' classics turned around. Watch for answers where only one of them takes a side.

choices.note: Tempting, because Malik talks about younger listeners. But he says they'd drift away from familiar works, and Rosa says nothing about them at all. Only one side takes a position.
Rosa says this, but Malik never denies it. He argues about the future audience, not current draws.
CORRECT. 'Only a small part for anything else' is Rosa's 'nearly all classics.' Rosa: yes. Malik wants a substantial share for new works: no.
Malik agrees: "Ticket sales certainly matter." An agreement point, not a disagreement.
Tempting, because Malik clearly thinks so: younger listeners are the future audience. But Rosa never mentions younger listeners or the long term. Only one side takes a position.

questions.stimulus: Gardener: This summer the tomato plants I mulched with straw produced far fewer split fruits than the unmulched tomato plants in my neighbor's plot did, although we set out our seedlings on the same day. Tomatoes split when soil moisture swings sharply, and a layer of straw keeps soil moisture steady. So mulching with straw reduces fruit splitting in tomatoes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the gardener's argument?
choices: The few unmulched tomato plants in the gardener's own plot split about as often as the neighbor's plants did.
Some tomato varieties are much more prone to splitting than others, whatever the moisture of the soil they grow in.
The gardener's neighbor harvested more tomatoes in total this summer than the gardener did, despite using no mulch.
Straw mulch also suppresses weeds that compete with tomato plants for water and nutrients in the soil.
Tomato splitting tends to be more widespread in summers with heavy rain late in the growing season.
questions.explanation: The comparison is between two different plots, so a difference other than mulch (variety, soil, watering) could explain the result. A shows that unmulched plants in the gardener's own plot split as often as the neighbor's, isolating the mulch as the difference. B raises a possible alternative cause and so, if anything, weakens; E would affect both plots alike; C and D are off the point.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mulching with straw reduces fruit splitting in tomatoes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The gardener's mulched plants split far less than the neighbor's unmulched plants; splitting comes from moisture swings, and straw steadies moisture.

breakdown.analysis: So the gardener's plot did better. Was it the straw, or the plot? Different gardens can differ in soil, variety, watering and shade. We need an answer that rules out the plot difference, ideally by comparing mulched and unmulched plants under the same conditions.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same plot, same gardener, no mulch: these plants split like the neighbor's. So the plot itself isn't what protected the mulched plants; the mulch is.
Tempting, because variety does matter. But it points to an alternative cause, which hurts the argument rather than helping it.
Total harvest isn't splitting. Interesting fact, but not relevant.
A second benefit of mulch, but the argument is about splitting, not weeds.
Rain would hit both plots the same way. It doesn't explain the difference or tie it to mulch.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago the town of Harwick converted its downtown parking garage into a public market, which has been crowded every weekend since it opened. Port Elm's downtown garage is about the same size as Harwick's and sits just as close to the town's main shopping street. Therefore, if Port Elm converts its garage into a market, that market will draw large crowds as well.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Converting Harwick's garage into a market cost considerably more than the town had originally budgeted for the project.
Port Elm has a somewhat larger population than Harwick does, and more of its residents work in the downtown area.
Harwick's market is the only one in its area, whereas two large markets already operate within a few miles of Port Elm.
Several vendors who sell at Harwick's market have said that they would be willing to sell at a market in Port Elm as well.
Weekend crowds at Harwick's market are somewhat larger in the summer months than they are during the rest of the year.
questions.explanation: The argument rests on an analogy: the two garages are alike in size and location, so a Port Elm market will be as popular as Harwick's. C points to a relevant difference: Harwick's market has no nearby competition, while Port Elm's would. A concerns cost rather than crowds, B and D if anything support the prediction, and E describes seasonal variation that applies to Harwick's market without distinguishing the towns.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A market in Port Elm's garage will draw large crowds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Harwick's converted garage market is crowded every weekend; Port Elm's garage is similar in size and location.

breakdown.analysis: Same size, same distance from the shops. Is that why Harwick's market is crowded? Maybe the crowds come for reasons that have nothing to do with the garage. An argument by analogy is only as good as the similarities that matter. We need a relevant difference between the towns, one that would keep crowds away from Port Elm's market.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Cost overruns say nothing about whether the market draws crowds.
Wrong direction. More people and more downtown workers would, if anything, help a Port Elm market.
CORRECT. Harwick's crowds may come because it has the only market around. Port Elm's would have to compete with two big ones nearby. That's a difference that matters.
This helps the argument. Willing vendors make a Port Elm market more likely to succeed.
Tempting, since it hints the crowds depend on something seasonal. But it's crowded every weekend anyway, and nothing here distinguishes Harwick from Port Elm.

questions.stimulus: Defendants in Dalton County who are awaiting trial and cannot afford bail remain in jail. A study of the county's criminal cases found that defendants held in jail before trial were more likely to plead guilty than were released defendants facing similar charges and comparably strong evidence. Many of the jailed defendants who pleaded guilty were sentenced to the time they had already served.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Being held in jail before trial is what led the jailed defendants in the study to plead guilty more often than released defendants did.
At least some of the jailed defendants who pleaded guilty would have been acquitted if their cases had instead gone to trial.
Released defendants in the county decide whether to plead guilty solely on the basis of the strength of the evidence against them.
For at least some defendants, something other than the strength of the case against them bears on the decision whether to plead guilty.
Some of the jailed defendants in the study who pleaded guilty would have received longer sentences had they instead been convicted at trial.
questions.explanation: Jailed and released defendants with comparably strong evidence pleaded guilty at different rates, so something besides the evidence affects some decisions to plead; D follows. A is the tempting overreach: jailed defendants are also the ones who could not afford bail, so detention itself need not be the cause. E is just as modestly worded as D but rests on trial sentences the facts never mention. B, though hedged, makes a claim about innocence the facts never address, and C's 'solely' is unsupported.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Defendants who can't afford bail stay in jail before trial; 2. jailed defendants pleaded guilty more often than released defendants with similar charges and similar evidence; 3. many jailed defendants who pleaded guilty got time served.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase exactly, but fact 2 is the key. Same charges, same strength of evidence, different plea rates. So the evidence can't be the whole story for everyone. Something else is in play. But be careful about naming what. Jailed defendants are also the ones who couldn't pay bail, so poverty, worse lawyers, or something else could be the difference. Watch for answers that pin it on one cause or blow it up into claims about innocence. And don't pick an answer just because it says 'some': check what the 'some' is about.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like what the study 'shows.' But the jailed group differs in another way: they couldn't afford bail. Money, or the lawyers money buys, could be the real difference. The facts support 'something besides evidence,' not this particular cause.

Hedged, but still unsupported. Pleading under pressure doesn't show that anyone would have won at trial. The facts say nothing about guilt or innocence; many pleaders may simply be guilty and want out.
Too strong. 'Solely' goes way past the facts. Released defendants could weigh many things; we only know the two groups differed.
CORRECT. Evidence was held comparable, yet the groups pleaded at different rates. So for some defendants a factor other than the evidence matters. 'At least some' keeps it safe.

Tempting, because it's hedged with 'some,' just like the right answer, and it offers a sensible-sounding reason to plead. But the facts say nothing about trial sentences. 'Time served' tells us what the pleaders got, not what a conviction would have cost them.

questions.stimulus: Sportswriter: Last season, each of the five starting players on the Harbor City basketball team was named to the regional all-star squad, an honor reserved for the region's best individual players. No other team in the region had more than two all-stars. So Harbor City must have been the best team in the region last season.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the sportswriter's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: treats the selection of Harbor City's starters for the all-star squad as evidence of their individual skill
takes for granted that the players were chosen for the all-star squad solely on the basis of their scoring
presumes that what is true of each member of a group must also be true of the group as a whole
overlooks the possibility that some players on other teams were better than some of Harbor City's starters
takes for granted that the regional all-star squad included at least one player from every team in the region
questions.explanation: The sportswriter moves from the excellence of each starter to the excellence of the team as a whole, though a team of strong individuals can still play poorly together; C describes this in general terms. A is tempting because the argument does treat the all-star picks as evidence of individual skill, but the premise defines the honor that way, so that step is sound. D is irrelevant: even if a few players elsewhere were better, the gap from players to team remains. Nothing presumes the players were chosen for scoring (B) or that every team had an all-star (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Harbor City was the best team in the region last season.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All five of its starters were all-stars, an honor for the best individual players; no other team had more than two.

breakdown.analysis: So every starter was great. Does that make the team great? Five stars who won't pass the ball can lose to a team of role players. This is the part-to-whole flaw: what's true of each part isn't automatically true of the whole. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the argument moves from the players to the team. Expect it to be stated abstractly.

choices.note: Tempting, because it describes something the argument really does. But it does it legitimately: the honor is 'reserved for the region's best individual players,' so all-star selection IS good evidence of individual skill. The flaw comes after that, in the jump from individuals to the team.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: He was voted class president, so he must be the most skilled debater in the school.

choices.note: Nothing in the argument depends on why the players were picked. Any basis for the honor leaves the same gap.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: She led the league in points, so she must be the league's best defender too.

choices.note: CORRECT. Group = the team; members = the starters. Each starter outstanding, so the team outstanding. That's the leap.
So? A few better players elsewhere wouldn't fix or create the problem. The argument's weakness is the move from individuals to the team, not the ranking of individuals.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our pitcher won the award, so no pitcher in the league is better than ours.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need this. Even if some teams had no all-stars, the gap from players to team remains.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our school had the most students on the honor list, so every school must have sent someone.

questions.stimulus: Health official: The rate of hospitalization for childhood asthma in Meade County is twice the rate in neighboring Ellis County. Meade's air contains far more diesel exhaust than Ellis's air does, mostly from the freight yards that ring Meade's largest town. Therefore, reducing the amount of diesel exhaust in Meade's air would lower Meade's rate of hospitalization for childhood asthma.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the health official's argument?
choices: Diesel exhaust is one of the causes of the initial onset of asthma in at least some of the children who live in Meade County.
Diesel exhaust in Meade's air contributes in some way to at least some of the hospitalizations for childhood asthma in Meade County.
At least some of the Meade County children hospitalized for asthma live near the freight yards that ring the county's largest town.
Children with asthma attacks are likelier to be taken to a hospital in Meade County than in Ellis County.
Ellis County has no freight yards or any other major source of diesel exhaust within its borders.
questions.explanation: If diesel exhaust played no part in any of Meade's childhood-asthma hospitalizations, cutting it would do nothing to the hospitalization rate, so the argument requires B. A is the tempting trap: it is as modest as B, but it names one particular route, causing asthma to begin, and exhaust could raise hospitalizations by worsening asthma children already have without ever causing it. C is modestly worded too, but the argument concerns exhaust in Meade's air generally, so the hospitalized children need not live near the freight yards. E is not needed (Ellis need only have less exhaust), and D would weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Reducing diesel exhaust in Meade would lower its childhood-asthma hospitalization rate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Meade's rate is twice Ellis's; Meade's air has far more diesel exhaust than Ellis's.

breakdown.analysis: Two counties differ in exhaust and in asthma hospitalizations. So cutting exhaust will cut hospitalizations? Only if exhaust has something to do with kids ending up in the hospital. It doesn't matter how: by giving kids asthma, by making attacks worse, or both. We need the minimal link: exhaust plays some part in at least some of those hospitalizations.

choices.note: Tempting: it's hedged like the right answer and it ties exhaust to asthma. But it insists on one route, giving children asthma in the first place. Exhaust could cut hospitalizations by worsening asthma kids already have, without ever causing it. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Diesel exhaust does not cause the onset of asthma in any of the children who live in Meade County.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: exhaust plays no part in any of Meade's childhood-asthma hospitalizations. Then reducing exhaust can't lower the hospitalization rate, and the argument collapses. It leaves open how exhaust contributes, so it holds whether exhaust starts asthma or worsens it.
choices.negation: Diesel exhaust in Meade's air contributes in no way to any of the hospitalizations for childhood asthma in Meade County.

choices.note: Tempting: it's hedged like the right answer and it ties the sick children to the exhaust source. But the official says Meade's air as a whole carries far more exhaust; children anywhere in the county can be exposed. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: None of the Meade County children hospitalized for asthma live near the freight yards that ring the county's largest town.

choices.note: Wrong direction. If Meade kids are just more likely to be hospitalized for the same attacks, that's an alternative explanation, which hurts the argument. And its negation doesn't hurt the argument either.
choices.negation: Children with asthma attacks are not more likely to be taken to a hospital in Meade than in Ellis.

choices.note: Too strong. Ellis just needs less exhaust than Meade, which the stimulus already says. Negating this changes nothing.
choices.negation: Ellis County has at least one freight yard or other major source of diesel exhaust.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Scholars disagree about whether the masons who built the region's medieval cathedrals worked from drawn plans. No such plans survive, but that is unsurprising: drawings were made on parchment, which was costly and was routinely scraped clean and reused. Moreover, the surviving accounts for a parish church built in the region by the same masons record repeated purchases of parchment "for the master's drawings." So the cathedral masons probably did work from drawn plans.
questions.stem: The historian's argument proceeds by
choices: treating the lack of any surviving evidence against a hypothesis as sufficient grounds for accepting that hypothesis
rejecting the view held by some scholars on the grounds that those scholars have misread the documents they cite
using records from a building project to draw a conclusion about how that same project was actually carried out
explaining why certain evidence would be missing and then reasoning from a similar case for which records exist
appealing to the testimony of medieval master builders to settle a question about which modern scholars disagree
questions.explanation: The historian first explains away the absence of surviving plans (parchment was scraped and reused), then uses records from a comparable project by the same masons to infer what the cathedral masons probably did. D describes both moves. A reverses the role of the missing evidence: the missing plans would be evidence for the hypothesis, and the historian merely explains their absence. C is the near-miss: the parish-church records are used to draw a conclusion about different projects, the cathedrals. B and E describe moves the historian never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The cathedral masons probably worked from drawn plans.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: No plans survive, but parchment was scraped and reused, so their loss is expected; accounts for a parish church built by the same masons record parchment bought for the master's drawings.

breakdown.analysis: Two moves here. 1. Defuse an objection: 'no plans survive' looks like evidence against drawn plans, so the historian explains why plans wouldn't survive even if they existed. 2. Build the case: a similar project by the same masons has records showing drawings were made. So: explain away missing evidence, then reason from a comparable, documented case. We need an answer with both halves. Watch the near-miss that gets the cases wrong: the records are from the parish church, the conclusion is about the cathedrals.

choices.note: Tempting, because the stimulus is all about missing evidence. But the missing plans would be evidence FOR the hypothesis, and the historian doesn't accept the hypothesis because of their absence; she explains the absence and then offers positive evidence.
choices.example: Example of this method: No one has ever proved that the old mill is unsafe, so we should accept that it is safe.

choices.note: The historian never says any scholar misread a document. She adds her own evidence; she doesn't attack anyone's reading.
choices.example: Example of this method: My opponents cite the 1802 letter, but they have misread its date, so their view should be rejected.

choices.note: Close, but wrong case. The records come from the parish church, and the conclusion is about the cathedrals. The historian reasons from one project to others, not to the same one.
choices.example: Example of this method: The church's own accounts list payments to glaziers, so its windows were made by hired glaziers.

choices.note: CORRECT. Scraped and reused parchment explains why the plans are missing; the parish church, built by the same masons, is the similar case whose records survive.
The phrase 'the master's drawings' comes from an account book, not from a master builder's testimony, and it's used as evidence about practice, not as an authority's verdict.
choices.example: Example of this method: The cathedral's chief mason wrote that plans were always used, and that settles the matter.

questions.stimulus: When the Ostrander Archive replaced its flatbed scanners with a high-speed book scanner, the staff time needed to digitize each manuscript fell by about 30 percent. Yet in the years after the new scanner was installed, the total staff time the archive devoted to digitizing manuscripts rose substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the total staff time the archive devoted to digitizing rose?
choices: In the first few weeks after the new scanner was installed, staff took longer per manuscript than they had with the flatbed scanners.
A few of the archive's staff members continued to use the old flatbed scanners for certain oversized manuscripts.
The time the archive's staff spent cataloging newly acquired manuscripts also rose substantially during those years.
The new scanner photographs both facing pages at once, sharply reducing the time spent turning and repositioning each manuscript.
The faster process made it practical to digitize thousands of manuscripts long judged too slow to scan, so far more were digitized.
questions.explanation: Less staff time per manuscript can still mean more staff time in total if many more manuscripts are digitized; E supplies that increase in volume. A is tempting, but a few slow weeks at the start cannot account for a substantial rise over years, during which each manuscript took less time. B's holdouts would only limit the savings, not push the total above its earlier level. C concerns cataloging rather than digitizing, and D explains only the per-manuscript savings.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The new scanner cut staff time per manuscript by about 30 percent, but total staff time spent digitizing rose.

breakdown.analysis: Per manuscript went down, total went up. How? Total = time per manuscript × number of manuscripts. If the number scanned grew enough, the total can rise even while each one takes less time. Watch the switch from a rate to a total. We need an answer that grows the number of manuscripts being digitized. Beware answers that make some manuscripts slower for a while: a short blip can't produce a rise that lasts for years.

choices.note: Tempting, because it does add staff time. But it's a few weeks, and the stimulus says per-manuscript time fell and the total rose over years. A short start-up slowdown can't explain a lasting, substantial rise.
Holdouts would make the savings smaller, but they were using flatbed scanners before too. They can't push the total above where it started.
Cataloging isn't digitizing. The puzzle is about staff time spent scanning manuscripts.
This explains the per-manuscript savings, one side of the puzzle. It does nothing to explain the rise.
CORRECT. Far more manuscripts, each taking less time. If the number scanned grew by more than enough to offset the 30 percent savings, the total rises.

questions.stimulus: Dr. Imani: Some residents want the city to stop fluoridating its water because a few people have reported mild tooth discoloration. But by that standard, the city would also have to stop chlorinating the water, since chlorine sometimes gives water an unpleasant taste. No one seriously proposes ending chlorination, which protects against waterborne disease. So mild discoloration alone is not a good reason to end fluoridation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in Dr. Imani's argument by the claim that the city would also have to stop chlorinating the water?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the claims about chlorine's taste and benefits are offered to support.
It is presented as an implication of the residents' standard, one that the argument treats as clearly unacceptable.
It is a premise offered in support of the residents' view that the city should stop fluoridating its water.
It is a claim that the argument concedes is true but maintains is irrelevant to the issue of fluoridation.
It is a subsidiary conclusion that is offered as the argument's only evidence that fluoridation causes no harm.
questions.explanation: Dr. Imani does not believe the city should stop chlorinating; she shows that the residents' standard (a minor side effect justifies ending a treatment) would require it, and since no one accepts that result, the standard fails. B describes this. A is wrong because the conclusion is the last sentence; C gets the direction backward; D and E misdescribe a claim the argument relies on and never offers as evidence of safety.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mild discoloration alone is not a good reason to end fluoridation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: By the residents' standard, the city would also have to stop chlorinating (chlorine sometimes tastes bad); no one seriously proposes ending chlorination.

breakdown.analysis: Does Dr. Imani think the city should stop chlorinating? No. That's the point. She takes the residents' rule (a minor side effect is enough to drop a treatment), applies it to chlorine, and gets a result everyone rejects. The author doesn't believe this claim. It's the absurd result used to sink the rule. We need an answer that says it's a consequence of the residents' standard that the argument rejects.

choices.note: The main conclusion is the last sentence, about discoloration not being a good reason. The chlorine claim supports that, not the other way around.
CORRECT. It's what the residents' standard would commit the city to, and the next sentence shows nobody accepts it. That's how the standard gets rejected.
Backwards. The claim is used against the residents' view, not for it.

Tempting, because Dr. Imani does think the 'by that standard' link holds. But she doesn't call it irrelevant; it's the heart of her argument, and she certainly doesn't accept that chlorination should end.
Wrong role and wrong job. The claim isn't supported by other premises, and the argument never tries to show fluoridation causes no harm at all.

questions.stimulus: Five years ago, bottom trawling was banned throughout Tolland Bay, ending a practice that had long torn up the seafloor where cod lay their eggs. Since the ban took effect, the number of juvenile cod counted in the bay's annual survey, which samples the same twenty sites each year, has tripled. Evidently, the ban has allowed the bay's cod population to recover.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Did the number of juvenile cod counted rise at every one of the twenty survey sites, or only at most of them?
Does bottom trawling also damage the seafloor habitat of fish species other than cod that live in the bay?
Were the twenty survey sites originally chosen because they had once held unusually many juvenile cod?
Before the ban, did any fishing method other than bottom trawling also disturb the seafloor where cod lay their eggs?
Has the number of cod larvae drifting into the bay from spawning grounds outside it changed since the ban took effect?
questions.explanation: The argument credits the ban, which protected the seafloor where cod spawn, for a tripling in juvenile cod counts. That works only if the extra juveniles came from spawning inside the bay. If far more eggs and larvae have been drifting in from outside, the rise may have nothing to do with the ban; if not, the ban looks responsible. E is the two-sided question. A and C probe the survey: a rise at all twenty sites or at most of them points the same way, and how the sites were picked long ago can't explain a tripling since the ban. D asks about other methods that disturbed the seafloor before the ban, which leaves the post-ban rise unexplained either way, and B concerns other species.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The trawling ban has allowed the bay's cod population to recover.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Trawling tore up cod spawning grounds; since the ban, juvenile cod counts at the same twenty sites have tripled.

breakdown.analysis: Counts tripled after the ban. But where did those young cod come from? The argument's mechanism is spawning on the protected seafloor inside the bay. Fish larvae drift. If a lot more of them have been riding currents in from spawning grounds elsewhere, the bay's juvenile count could triple with the ban doing nothing. We need a question about some other source of the juveniles. Ask it both ways: more inflow, the ban loses credit; same inflow, the ban looks like the cause. Watch for questions about the survey that sound methodical but wouldn't change your view either way.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like checking the data. But either answer leaves the argument where it was. A tripling at most sites or at all of them points the same way.
Other species are out of scope. The argument is about whether the ban let the cod recover, and harm to other fish doesn't bear on that.

Tempting, since site selection sounds like a sampling problem. But the same sites were counted before and after the ban, and how they were picked long ago can't explain why counts tripled in the last five years.

Tempting, because it hints at another cause of habitat damage. But whatever else disturbed the seafloor before the ban, counts tripled after it. A 'yes' doesn't explain the rise, and a 'no' doesn't add to the case. Neither answer moves the argument.

CORRECT. The argument assumes the new juveniles were spawned on the bay's own seafloor. If far more young cod have been drifting in from elsewhere, the tripling may owe nothing to the ban. If inflow is unchanged, the ban-protected spawning grounds look responsible. Either answer matters.

questions.stimulus: The Oakmere Neighborhood Association mailed a questionnaire to all 600 households in the neighborhood, asking whether Oakmere Avenue should be closed to cars and made a pedestrian-only street. Of the 240 households that returned the questionnaire, 85 percent favored the change. Since every household in the neighborhood received the questionnaire, most of the neighborhood's households must favor closing the avenue to cars.
questions.stem: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: relies on a sample that is too small to represent the views of a neighborhood of 600 households
takes for granted that households that favored the change when they responded will still favor it after the avenue is closed
takes for granted that the households that returned the questionnaire think like those that did not
fails to consider that some households in the neighborhood may never have received the association's questionnaire
overlooks the possibility that some households that favored closing the avenue did not fully understand what the change would involve
questions.explanation: Only 240 of 600 households answered, so the 85 percent describes respondents, not the neighborhood. Households that bothered to reply, perhaps because they feel strongly about the avenue, may differ from the 360 that did not; C names this. D is the near-miss: it also concerns who took part, but the argument states that every household received the questionnaire, so the problem is who chose to answer, not who was asked. A is tempting but misplaces the problem: 240 of 600 is a large sample, and what matters is who chose to answer, not how many. B shifts to future attitudes the conclusion never mentions, and E questions how well households understood the change, which doesn't bear on whether they favor it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the neighborhood's households favor closing the avenue to cars.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All 600 households got the questionnaire; 240 returned it; 85 percent of those favored the change.

breakdown.analysis: Everyone got it. So what? Only 240 answered. Who answers a questionnaire about closing a street? People who care, and people who care may lean one way. Do the math: 85 percent of 240 is 204 households, about a third of 600. To get 'most,' the argument needs the 360 silent households to look like the ones that replied. We need an answer that says the argument presumes respondents and non-respondents think alike. The trap will talk about who RECEIVED the questionnaire; the argument already covered that.

choices.note: Tempting, because something IS wrong with the sample. But 240 of 600 households is a big sample, not a small one. The trouble is who chose to answer, not how many did. A sample of 240 that picked itself can mislead; a random 240 wouldn't.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: I asked three of the 600 households, and all three favor the change, so most households must favor it.

choices.note: The conclusion is about what households favor now, not whether they'll keep favoring it once the street is closed. No time shift happens in the argument.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most residents favor the new park, so they'll still be glad of it ten years after it opens.

choices.note: CORRECT. The 85 percent comes from those who chose to reply. Getting to "most of all households" requires the non-repliers to share their views, and nothing supports that.

Tempting, because it's also about who took part. But the argument states that every household received the questionnaire. You can't attack a premise in a flaw answer; the gap is between those who got it and those who answered.

Tempting, since it questions the quality of the responses. But the conclusion is about what households favor, not about whether they understand it. A household that favors the change for a muddled reason still favors it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most voters chose the measure, so most voters must understand its fine print.

questions.stimulus: Hotel manager: We should stop leaving a complimentary printed newspaper outside each guest room every morning. The papers cost us a considerable sum each year, and our housekeepers report that most of them are left unread. So ending the practice would save money without making our guests any less satisfied with their stays.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the hotel manager's argument?
choices: A count conducted by the hotel confirmed that well over half of the newspapers left outside guest rooms are never opened.
Several other hotels in the city have recently stopped leaving free printed newspapers outside their guests' rooms.
Most guests who do read the newspapers left outside their rooms can readily get the same news on their own devices.
Guests who stay at the hotel on business are more likely than other guests to read the newspaper left outside their room.
The hotel spends less on the newspapers each year than it spends on the toiletries it provides in each guest room.
questions.explanation: That most papers go unread shows only that most guests won't miss them; the guests who do read them might. C addresses exactly those readers: they can get the news elsewhere with no effort, so losing the paper is unlikely to reduce their satisfaction. A is the trap: it confirms a premise the argument already has, and says nothing about the readers. B appeals to what other hotels do, D if anything singles out a group that might be disappointed, and E bears on the size of the savings, not on satisfaction.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ending newspaper delivery would save money without making guests any less satisfied.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The papers cost a lot; most are left unread.

breakdown.analysis: Most papers go unread. Fine. What about the ones that are read? 'Most' leaves a minority, and the conclusion says NO loss in satisfaction. If the guests who read the paper love it, they'll be unhappy. We need something that says those readers won't miss it. Most students pick (A) because it backs up the housekeepers' report. It fails because the argument already grants that most papers go unread; proving it again doesn't touch the readers. Don't strengthen a premise the argument already has.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It confirms the 'most are unread' premise. But that premise was never in doubt, and the gap is about the minority who read the paper.
What other hotels do isn't evidence about this hotel's guests' satisfaction. Popularity isn't proof.
CORRECT. The readers are the only guests who could be disappointed, and they can get the same news on their own devices. That makes "no less satisfied" much more plausible.
Wrong direction, if anything. It points to a group of guests who do value the paper. It doesn't show they won't mind losing it.
This is about how much money is saved. Even if the savings are smaller than the toiletry budget, they're still savings, and nothing here touches satisfaction.

questions.stimulus: Music teacher: Students who practice an instrument in many short sessions each week generally improve faster than students who put in the same total amount of practice time in a few long sessions. Yet most of my students practice in a few long sessions each week, because they find those easier to fit around school, sports, and part-time jobs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the music teacher's statements?
choices: Most of the teacher's students would improve faster than they now do if they put in the same total practice time in many short sessions instead.
At least some of the teacher's students arrange their practice in a way that typically yields slower progress than another arrangement of the same total time.
Most of the teacher's students would practice in many short sessions each week if their schedules allowed them to do so.
At least one of the teacher's students who practices in many short sessions improves faster than all of her students who practice in a few long sessions.
Some of the teacher's students who have part-time jobs put in less total practice time each week than her other students do.
questions.explanation: Short sessions generally beat long ones for equal total time, and most of the teacher's students use long sessions, so at least some of her students use the arrangement that typically yields slower progress; B says exactly that in abstract terms. A is the trap: it uses the stimulus's own words but turns a generalization ('generally') into a claim about what would happen to most of one teacher's students, who may be exceptions. C invents a preference, D, though it speaks of only one student, pits that student against every long-session student, which 'generally' cannot support, and E is hedged like B but about total practice time, on which the stimulus is silent.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. For the same total time, many short sessions generally beat a few long ones; 2. Most of the teacher's students practice in a few long sessions; 3. They do so because long sessions fit their schedules.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, but the two facts combine: most of her students use the setup that generally loses. So at least some of her students are on the slower track as a rule. Watch the word 'generally.' It describes students in general, not what would happen to each student, or even to most of this teacher's students. An answer that predicts their individual results claims more than the facts give.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It's built from the stimulus's own words. But 'generally improve faster' is a statement about students as a whole. This teacher's students could be exceptions: maybe long sessions suit them. 'Most of her students would improve faster' needs more than a generalization.

CORRECT. Most of her students use a few long sessions; for equal time, that arrangement typically yields slower progress than many short ones. So at least some of her students practice the typically slower way. It's abstract and modest, which is why it's safe.
We don't know what they'd prefer. They find long sessions easier to fit in; that doesn't mean they'd switch if schedules opened up.

Hedged at the front ('at least one'), but the back half is universal: faster than ALL her long-session students. 'Generally' allows exceptions, so a long-session student could outpace every short-session one. We also don't know she has any short-session students.
Hedged, so it looks safe. But the stimulus never compares how much total time different students put in; jobs are mentioned only as a reason long sessions are easier to schedule.

questions.stimulus: In the twelve months after Vantor Motors introduced its new compact, owners filed fewer than one warranty claim for every twenty compacts sold during that period. No earlier Vantor model had so low a claim rate in its own first twelve months on the market. An industry analyst concludes that the new compact is more reliable than any car Vantor has previously produced.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the analyst's argument?
choices: Owners of the new compact, like owners of Vantor's earlier models, sometimes file warranty claims for damage that their own misuse caused.
Most first-year sales of the new compact came in the year's final two months; earlier models' first-year sales were spread evenly across the year.
The new compact's warranty covers more of the car's components than the warranties on any of Vantor's earlier models covered.
Most of the claims filed on the new compact during its first twelve months concerned faults serious enough to leave the car undrivable until repaired.
Several rival manufacturers' compact cars had lower claim rates in their first twelve months on the market than Vantor's new compact had.
questions.explanation: The claim rate counts claims filed during the twelve months against cars sold during those months. If most compacts were sold in the final two months, most had only weeks in which to break down, while earlier models' cars averaged about half a year of use in the same window; B explains the low rate without any gain in reliability. D is the main trap: serious faults sound like unreliability, but we know nothing about the severity of earlier models' claims, so it sets up no comparison. C, if anything, strengthens the argument, since broader coverage should produce more claims. A applies equally to all models, and E concerns rival makers, while the conclusion compares Vantor cars only.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new compact is more reliable than any earlier Vantor car.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Its claims per car sold in its first twelve months were lower than any earlier model's in their first twelve months.

breakdown.analysis: Is a low claim rate the same as a reliable car? Only if each car had the same chance to break and be claimed on. Look at how the rate is built: claims filed in the twelve months, divided by cars sold in those twelve months. A car sold in week 50 has had two weeks to fail. We need an answer that shows the compact's cars had less time, or less occasion, to generate claims. It will look like a fact about sales, not about quality.

choices.note: Tempting, because misuse claims distort the numbers. But it says this happens with the compact LIKE the earlier models. A distortion that hits every model equally doesn't change the comparison.

CORRECT. If most compacts were bought in the last two months, most had only weeks in which to develop a fault before the count closed; earlier models' cars averaged about six months. The low rate reflects less time on the road, not a better car.
This points the wrong way. Broader coverage means more problems qualify for a claim, so the compact's low rate is even more impressive. That strengthens the analyst.

Tempting, and the main trap. Breakdowns that leave the car undrivable sound like unreliability. But we're told nothing about how serious the earlier models' claims were, so there's no comparison. The compact can have serious claims and still have the fewest of them.
So? The conclusion compares the compact only with other Vantor cars. Rivals doing better doesn't touch that.

questions.stimulus: A teacher should grant a student an extension on a graded assignment only if the student has not already received an extension on a graded assignment that term, unless the new request is due to a documented illness. Moreover, when the assignment is a group project, such an extension should be granted only after the student's group members have been told of it.
questions.stem: The principle stated above most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Ortiz has received no extensions this term, and the other members of his project group have been told of his request. So his teacher should grant Ortiz an extension.
Pryce already received an extension on a graded essay this term, but her current request, for her individual lab report, is due to a documented illness. So her teacher should not grant it.
Lam already received an extension on a graded report this term, but his request for more time on his individual essay is due to a documented illness. So Lam's teacher should grant it.
Hale already had one extension this term, but his request on his group's graded project is due to a documented illness. His group has not been told of it, so granting it now would be premature.
Reyes has had no extensions this term, and the members of her project group were told of her request and objected to it. So her teacher should not grant Reyes the extension.
questions.explanation: Both rules state necessary conditions, so the principle can justify only withholding an extension, and only when a condition fails. Hale's illness lifts the first bar, but his request concerns a group project whose members have not been told, so the second rule says not yet; D is justified. A and C treat the conditions (or the illness exception) as sufficient for granting. B misreads the exception: illness removes the bar on a second extension, so nothing in the principle supports refusing Pryce. E rests on the group's objection, which the principle never mentions.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Grant an extension → no earlier graded extension this term, UNLESS the request is due to documented illness. Group project: grant → group members told first.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the argument whose conclusion the principle forces.

breakdown.analysis: Both rules are 'only if' rules. They tell you when a teacher must NOT grant (yet), never when a teacher must grant. So any answer concluding 'should grant' is out unless something else forces it. Then the 'unless' clause: documented illness removes the first bar. It doesn't create a right to the extension, and it doesn't touch the group rule. We need a conclusion against granting that comes from a condition that actually fails.

choices.note: Tempting. Ortiz meets every condition. But meeting necessary conditions doesn't make granting required. The principle says when not to grant, never when to grant.
This misreads the 'unless.' Pryce's illness lifts the bar on a second extension, and her report is individual, so no condition fails. The principle gives no reason to refuse her.
Tempting, because the illness does remove the bar on a second extension. But removing a bar isn't the same as requiring the grant. 'Should grant' still doesn't follow.

CORRECT. The illness takes care of the first rule, which is a distraction. The project is a group project and the members haven't been told, so the second rule says the extension may not be granted yet. 'Premature' is exactly what the principle supports.
The group's objection is irrelevant. The rule requires that members be told, not that they agree. And Reyes meets both conditions, so there's no basis for refusing.

questions.stimulus: Sea otters returned to Merrow Sound twelve years ago, after an absence of several decades. Otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins graze on kelp. In the years since the otters' return, the kelp forests in the sound have more than doubled in area. Thus, the otters' return is probably the main reason that the kelp forests have expanded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Sea otters eat more of the sound's sea urchins than does any other predator that lives in or passes through the sound.
Before the otters returned, animals that otters eat were among the factors limiting the size of the sound's kelp forests.
At least some of the sound's sea urchins were eaten by the returning otters within the first two years after the otters came back.
Grazing by sea urchins was the chief factor limiting the spread of the sound's kelp forests in the years before the otters returned.
Kelp forests in nearby waters to which otters have not returned did not also double in area during the past twelve years.
questions.explanation: The proposed mechanism is otters → fewer urchins → more kelp. That works only if the otters' prey had actually been holding the kelp back before the otters returned; if nothing the otters eat was limiting the kelp, removing it could not let the kelp expand. B states this with a stand-in description ('animals that otters eat'). D is the near-miss: urchin grazing need only be one limiting factor, not the chief one, for the otters to be the main reason for the change. E would strengthen the argument, but if nearby kelp doubled too, the otters could still be the main cause here. C fixes a timetable the argument doesn't need, and A compares predators the argument never ranks.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The otters' return is probably the main reason the sound's kelp forests expanded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Otters eat urchins; urchins graze kelp; the otters returned twelve years ago and the kelp has since doubled.

breakdown.analysis: Otters eat urchins, and urchins eat kelp. Does that mean removing urchins frees the kelp? Only if the urchins were actually keeping it down. If something else, like light or nutrients, capped the kelp entirely, fewer urchins would change nothing. We need the modest link: before the otters came back, the urchins were part of what held the kelp back. Expect it in roundabout wording.

choices.note: Not required. Another predator could eat more urchins; the otters' added eating can still be what tipped the balance.
choices.negation: Some other predator in the sound eats more of its sea urchins than the otters do.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Animals that otters eat' are the urchins. Negate it: nothing the otters eat was holding the kelp back. Then the otters' return can't explain the kelp's expansion, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Before the otters returned, no animal that otters eat was among the factors limiting the size of the kelp forests.

choices.note: Hedged like the right answer, so it feels safe. But the timing isn't needed. If the otters only began to cut urchin numbers in year three, they could still be the main reason the kelp has since doubled.
choices.negation: None of the sound's sea urchins were eaten by the returning otters within the first two years after the otters came back.

choices.note: Tempting: the right idea at the wrong strength. Urchins needn't be the chief limit. If the chief limit stayed constant, the change in urchins could still account for most of the change in kelp.
choices.negation: Grazing by sea urchins was not the chief factor limiting the spread of the kelp forests before the otters returned.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the comparison you'd want if you were testing the claim, and it would strengthen the argument. But it isn't required. If kelp nearby also doubled, the cause there could be different, and the otters could still be the main reason here. That weakens the argument; it doesn't destroy it.
choices.negation: Kelp forests in nearby otter-free waters also doubled in area during the past twelve years.

questions.stimulus: Under the Ridgefield Swim Club's rules, any swimmer who breaks a club record during the season earns an invitation to the regional training camp. Odile, who swims for Ridgefield, received an invitation to this year's camp, and she trained harder this season than ever before. So Odile must have broken a club record this season.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Every chef who completes the Marlow Institute's program learns to make stock from scratch. Petra never completed that program, even though she enrolled in it. So Petra must not know how to make stock from scratch.
Every apartment in the Elgin Building comes with a private balcony. Dev's apartment, which he has rented for six years, has no private balcony. So Dev's apartment must not be in the Elgin Building.

Most volunteers who attend the orientation session stay with the literacy program for a full year. Tomas attended this spring's orientation session. So Tomas will probably stay with the program for a full year.
Yusuf must have spent over $100 on his last visit to Fenwick's, since he left the store with a discount coupon, and Fenwick's gives one to every customer who spends over $100 in a single visit.

Only applicants who pass the entrance exam are admitted to Whitcombe Academy. Lena, who studied for the exam all summer, was admitted to Whitcombe Academy this fall. So Lena must have passed the entrance exam.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a sufficient condition as necessary: breaking a record guarantees an invitation, but an invitation could come for other reasons.
