D makes the same move, inferring big spending from the coupon, though it states its conclusion first and has no filler detail. E is the trap: it copies the original's order and even its irrelevant detail about hard work, but 'only' makes passing the exam necessary for admission, so its conclusion follows. A negates the condition instead of reversing it, B is a valid contrapositive, and C is a reasonable probabilistic inference.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Odile must have broken a club record.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Breaks a record → invited; Odile was invited (and trained hard).

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X → Y; this one has Y; so this one must have X (affirming the consequent). The training detail is filler.

breakdown.analysis: Breaks a record → invited. Odile was invited. So she broke a record? Not necessarily: there may be other ways to earn an invitation, like a coach's pick or a fast time at a meet. The training detail is filler. We need the same move: X → Y; Y; so X. Most students pick (E) because it looks like a carbon copy, right down to the hard-work filler. But "only applicants who pass are admitted" means admitted → passed. Lena was admitted, so she passed. That's valid, so it can't match a flawed argument. Read "only" carefully: it marks the necessary condition. The right answer, (D), hides by leading with its conclusion; rearrange it and it's the same skeleton.

choices.note: A different error: X → Y; not X; so not Y (denying the antecedent). Petra could have learned to make stock somewhere else.
Valid. Every Elgin apartment has a balcony; Dev's doesn't; so it isn't in the Elgin Building. That's a correct contrapositive.
A modest "probably" drawn from a "most" premise. That's reasonable, not the same flaw.
CORRECT. Rearranged: spends over $100 → coupon; Yusuf got a coupon; so he spent over $100. Same reversal. Coupons might also go out for birthdays or promotions.

Tempting, and the main trap. Same order, same filler. But "only applicants who pass are admitted" makes passing necessary for admission, so admission proves passing. Valid, so it doesn't share the original's flaw.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Some blame outdoor cats for the decline in the region's songbird populations. But over the past decade, songbird numbers have fallen most steeply in the region's remote forests, where outdoor cats are rare, and least steeply in its suburbs, where outdoor cats are common. So outdoor cats are not responsible for any part of the decline.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the ecologist's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: infers that one phenomenon causes another merely from the fact that the two phenomena tend to occur together
overlooks the possibility that something other than outdoor cats is responsible for the steep decline in the remote forests
dismisses the view of those who blame outdoor cats without first examining the evidence on which that view is based
fails to consider that outdoor cats may be responsible for songbird declines in regions other than the one it discusses
takes for granted that, without outdoor cats, suburban songbird numbers would have fallen just as much as they did
questions.explanation: The pattern across places shows that cats are not the main driver of the regional decline, but the conclusion denies that they are responsible for any part of it. That follows only if suburban songbirds would have declined just as much without cats; perhaps the suburbs lack whatever is devastating the forests, and cats account for much of their milder decline. E identifies this. B is the near-miss: the argument is fully compatible with some other cause in the forests, and in fact implicitly grants one. A describes inferring causation from correlation, the reverse of what the ecologist does. C and D raise issues the conclusion does not depend on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Outdoor cats are not responsible for any part of the songbird decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The decline is steepest in remote forests, where cats are rare, and mildest in suburbs, where cats are common.

breakdown.analysis: Not responsible for ANY part? The data show cats aren't the big story: the worst losses are where cats are scarce. But something else could be hammering the forests (logging, say) while sparing the suburbs, and cats could be causing most of the smaller suburban decline. The argument only works if the suburbs would have lost just as many birds with no cats around. That's a hidden counterfactual, and it's the flaw. Most students pick (B) because 'overlooks another cause' is the reflex flaw. It fails because another cause in the forests doesn't hurt the argument at all; the ecologist is practically pointing to one. Another trap, (A), names the textbook correlation flaw, but this argument goes the other way: it denies a cause because the correlation is missing.

choices.note: Tempting because causation is on the table, but this is the reverse of what happens. The ecologist infers NO causal link from a pattern that doesn't fit; nobody here infers a cause from things occurring together.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in July, so ice cream causes drowning.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It uses the stimulus's own words. But some other cause in the forests is perfectly consistent with the argument; the steep forest decline practically demands one. Overlooking it does no harm. The problem is the suburbs, not the forests.
The ecologist doesn't need to review the other side's evidence to make this argument. The flaw is in what her own evidence can show.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Some say the bridge is unsafe, but I haven't looked at their engineering report, and I say it's fine.

choices.note: Out of scope. The conclusion is only about this region's decline.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Cats haven't harmed birds here, so they don't harm birds anywhere.

choices.note: CORRECT. To say cats caused none of the decline, the argument needs the suburbs to have lost just as many birds without cats. If cats caused most of the suburban losses, they're responsible for part of the decline after all.

questions.stimulus: Legal scholar: A court ruling deserves public confidence only if it is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow. But a ruling that turns on a dispute among specialists cannot be explained in such terms unless the court sets out the specialists' competing views in plain language. In the Marsh case, the appellate court did not set out in plain language the views of either side's forensic experts. So the Marsh ruling does not deserve public confidence.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the legal scholar's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any court ruling that sets out specialists' competing views in plain language is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow.
A court ruling that is explained in terms that ordinary citizens can follow deserves the confidence of the public.
What the appellate court decided in the Marsh case depended on which side's forensic experts had the better of their dispute.
The forensic experts in the Marsh case disagreed with one another about matters that ordinary citizens could not easily follow.
Most court rulings that turn on a dispute among specialists fail to set out the specialists' views in plain language.
questions.explanation: The second rule applies only to a ruling that turns on a dispute among specialists. C says, in other words, that the Marsh ruling did: the outcome depended on which side's forensic experts were right. Then, since the experts' views were not set out plainly, the ruling was not explained in followable terms, and by the first rule it does not deserve confidence. D is the trap: it shows the experts disagreed, but not that the ruling turned on their dispute, so the second rule is never triggered. A and B reverse the stated conditionals, and E's 'most' says nothing about this case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Marsh ruling does not deserve public confidence.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Deserves confidence → explained in followable terms; for a ruling that turns on a specialist dispute, followable → specialists' views set out plainly; the Marsh court did not set out either side's forensic experts' views plainly.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Rule 2, contrapositive: turns on a specialist dispute AND views not set out plainly → not followable. Rule 1, contrapositive: not followable → no confidence. Marsh: views not set out plainly. What's missing? Whether the Marsh ruling turned on a dispute among specialists at all. Without that, rule 2 never kicks in. Full chain: Marsh turned on expert dispute + views not set out → not followable → no confidence. Most students pick (D) because it puts the experts in a dispute about hard matters, which feels like the missing piece. It fails because experts disagreeing isn't the ruling turning on their disagreement; the court could have decided on other grounds. (C) hides behind a paraphrase: "depended on which side's experts had the better of their dispute" means "turned on a dispute among specialists."

choices.note: Reverses rule 2. Setting out the views plainly is necessary for a followable explanation; this makes it sufficient. It's also about rulings that DO set them out, and Marsh didn't.
Reverses rule 1. Being followable is necessary for confidence, not sufficient. And it only tells us about followable rulings, while we're trying to show Marsh isn't one.
CORRECT. If the decision depended on which experts were right, the ruling turned on a specialist dispute. Rule 2 plus the unexplained views → not followable; rule 1 → no public confidence.

Tempting, and the main trap. There's a dispute in the case, but rule 2 needs the RULING to turn on it. The court might have decided Marsh on a procedural point. Then rule 2 doesn't apply and the conclusion doesn't follow.
"Most" rulings tells us nothing about Marsh. A sufficient assumption has to lock in this case.

questions.stimulus: Under the rules of the consulting firm Kessler & Doyle, a proposal is sent to the client once both the firm's finance committee and its legal department have approved it. The finance committee considers a proposal only after the legal department has reviewed it, and the legal department has never rejected a proposal it has reviewed. Last week the finance committee approved the Hartwell proposal. So the Hartwell proposal will be sent to the client.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: mistakes a condition that is sufficient for a proposal to be sent to the client for one that is necessary for it to be sent
treats the legal department's review of a proposal as enough to ensure that the finance committee will consider that proposal
takes for granted that the finance committee would not approve a proposal that the legal department had rejected
overlooks the possibility that the finance committee approved the Hartwell proposal before the legal department had reviewed it
infers that the legal department approved the Hartwell proposal merely from the fact that the department did not reject it
questions.explanation: Finance approved Hartwell, so legal must already have reviewed it, and since legal has never rejected a proposal, it did not reject Hartwell. But the sending rule requires legal's approval, and a review can end in neither approval nor rejection: the proposal could still be pending or sent back for revision. E names this inference from 'not rejected' to 'approved.' A names a familiar necessary-sufficient flaw that the argument doesn't commit: it uses the sending rule correctly, as sufficient. B reverses the 'only after' premise, which the argument never does. C is not assumed, since legal has rejected nothing for finance to approve. D contradicts the premise that finance considers only proposals legal has already reviewed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Hartwell proposal will be sent to the client.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Finance approval + legal approval → sent; finance considers a proposal → legal already reviewed it; legal has never rejected a proposal it reviewed; finance approved Hartwell last week.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: finance approved Hartwell → legal reviewed it → legal didn't reject it → ... legal approved it? Not rejecting isn't approving. A review can end with the proposal on hold, sent back for changes, or still waiting for a decision. The sending rule needs legal's APPROVAL, and nothing says legal gave it. It's like saying: my editor has never rejected a story I filed, so the one I filed today runs tomorrow. Maybe it's still on her desk. Watch the switch from 'not rejected' to 'approved.' We need an answer that says the argument treats them as the same. Expect a necessary-versus-sufficient trap; check whether the argument actually commits it.

choices.note: Tempting, because conditional rules invite this answer. But the argument uses the rule the right way: both approvals are sufficient for sending, and the argument concludes 'will be sent' from both approvals. No mix-up.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Proposals approved by both bodies are sent, and the Ames proposal was sent, so both bodies must have approved it.

choices.note: This reverses the premise. Legal review is required before finance considers a proposal; the argument never treats review as guaranteeing consideration. It doesn't need to: finance did consider Hartwell.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Finance considers only reviewed proposals, and legal reviewed the Ames proposal, so finance will consider it.

choices.note: Tempting, since it uses the same word, 'rejected,' and sounds like a hidden assumption. But the argument doesn't need it: legal has never rejected anything, so there's no rejected proposal for finance to approve. The real gap is between not rejecting and approving.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Finance would never approve a proposal legal rejected, so every proposal finance approves is one legal approved.

choices.note: This contradicts a premise. Finance considers a proposal only after legal has reviewed it, so Hartwell's legal review came first. A flaw answer can't fault the argument for trusting its own premises.

CORRECT. Legal reviewed Hartwell and, given its record, didn't reject it. But the rule needs legal's approval, and a proposal can be reviewed and still be pending or returned for revisions. The argument concludes approval from the mere absence of rejection.

questions.stimulus: Most commuters in Pell City choose between driving downtown and taking the train mainly on the basis of total travel time. The city plans to add express trains that would cut ten minutes from the train trip downtown. It also plans to close two of the three parking lots at Maple Street, the station that most train commuters drive to and the one that people who now drive downtown would mostly use if they switched to the train. Commuters who cannot quickly find parking there could easily lose ten minutes. So ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the city should consider postponing the closing of the two Maple Street lots until the express trains have begun running
the express trains could make the trip downtown longer for some of the commuters who board at the Maple Street station
fewer commuters will take the train downtown once two of the three parking lots at the Maple Street station have closed
the city's plans, taken together, need not make the train any more attractive to those who now drive all the way downtown
commuters who now take the train may come to care more about parking near the station than about the length of the trip itself
questions.explanation: Commuters weigh total travel time; the express trains cut ten minutes, but at the station most rail commuters drive to, lost parking could eat those ten minutes. The stimulus adds that drivers who switched would mostly use that station too, so the combined plans may leave the train no faster for them; D follows, hedged as the evidence allows. B is hedged but pins lost time on the express trains, which only save time, and C turns 'could easily lose' into a firm outcome. A recommends a policy the argument doesn't weigh, however cautiously, and E is hedged like D but posits a change in what commuters value, which nothing supports.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most commuters choose train vs. car by total travel time; 2. Express trains would save ten minutes on the train; 3. Two of three lots will close at Maple Street, where most train commuters drive to board and where switching drivers would mostly board; 4. Failing to park quickly could cost ten minutes.

breakdown.analysis: What is the author driving at? The express trains are supposed to make the train faster. But the parking closures could hand back the time saved, for the very people who drive to the station. And who would a new rider be? Someone who now drives downtown, and the stimulus says those people would mostly use Maple Street. So the plans together may not tip the time comparison for drivers at all. The 'could' in fact 4 means the right answer should be hedged, but hedging alone won't pick it out: several choices are hedged. Check what each one actually claims, and watch for answers that turn 'could' into 'will.'

choices.note: Hedged ('consider'), but still a recommendation. The argument never weighs the timing of the two plans or recommends anything, and postponing would only delay the same combination. A 'should' conclusion needs a value premise this argument lacks.

Tempting, because it's hedged and points at Maple Street commuters. But it blames the wrong plan. The express trains cut ten minutes; they can't lengthen anyone's trip. It's the lot closures that could cost time.
Too strong. Even commuters who lose the ten minutes are no worse off than now, as far as we know. Nothing shows anyone will leave the train.

CORRECT. The ten-minute gain may vanish for those who drive to Maple Street, and the stimulus says drivers who switched would mostly be among them. So the plans, taken together, may not make the train any faster for drivers, the people the express trains would need to win over. 'Need not' matches the 'could' in the evidence.
Hedged, so it looks careful. But the stimulus says commuters decide on total travel time and gives no reason that would change. Parking matters only as part of that total.

questions.stimulus: Museum director: The Halvorsen Museum should not lend its fragile, one-of-a-kind medieval tapestry to the touring exhibition, even though the tour would let many thousands of people see the tapestry who otherwise never would. Each move exposes the tapestry to a small but real risk of irreparable damage, and once it is damaged, no future visitor will ever see it as it is now.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the museum director's argument?
choices: One should not offer people an opportunity now if doing so carries any chance of permanently denying that opportunity to everyone who comes later.
A museum should not lend a fragile work to any exhibition if moving the work would expose it to a significant risk of irreparable damage.
A museum should give the interests of its future visitors as much weight as it gives the interests of the people who would see its works today.
Museums should make their works accessible to as many people as possible, unless doing so would expose the works to some risk of harm.
A fragile, one-of-a-kind work should be lent only to exhibitions whose organizers have recognized expertise in safely transporting and conserving such works.
questions.explanation: The director refuses to lend even though thousands would see the tapestry, because any damage would permanently deny future visitors the chance to see it as it is now. A covers this: the tour offers people now the chance to see the tapestry and carries some chance of permanently denying that chance to everyone later. B is the near-miss: the director calls the risk small, not significant. D's 'unless' clause only releases museums from the duty to share; it never says they should refuse. C's equal weighting leaves the thousands of present viewers on the scale, so it doesn't favor refusal. E's condition can't be checked from the facts.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The museum should not lend the tapestry to the touring exhibition.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The tour would let thousands see it; each move carries a small but real risk of irreparable damage; once damaged, no future visitor will see it as it is now.

breakdown.analysis: The director concedes the benefit is large and the risk is small. So why refuse? Because the loss would be permanent and would fall on everyone after. We need a principle that says a small chance of permanent loss to the future beats a present benefit. Don't expect it to mention museums or tapestries; it may be stated as a rule about opportunities in general. Watch the risk level: 'small but real.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Translate: the opportunity = seeing the tapestry as it now is. The tour offers it to people now, and the small but real risk is a chance of permanently denying it to all later visitors. The principle says don't offer it, which is the director's conclusion.
Tempting, and the main trap. It's about museums, fragile works and irreparable damage. But it requires a SIGNIFICANT risk, and the director says the risk is small. It doesn't apply.

Equal weight sounds like the director's concern for future visitors. But equal weighting puts many thousands of present viewers against a small risk, so it may favor lending. It doesn't yield the conclusion.

Tempting, because the 'unless' clause seems to fit: the tour carries some risk. But the clause only removes the duty to maximize access. Not being required to lend isn't the same as being required not to lend.
We don't know who organized the tour or what expertise they have, so this can't settle anything here. And the director's reason is the risk of any move, not who handles the tapestry.

questions.stimulus: Most of the paintings in the Varga Museum's collection that were cleaned with a new solvent last year showed no clouding of their varnish afterward. Every painting in the collection that showed no such clouding was approved for loan to other museums. So some of the paintings that were cleaned with the new solvent were approved for loan.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most of the musicians in the Fairview orchestra studied at a conservatory. Most musicians who studied at a conservatory can sight-read difficult scores. So some musicians in the Fairview orchestra can sight-read difficult scores.

Every bicycle sold at Corliss Cycles comes with a one-year warranty. Most bicycles that come with a one-year warranty are made overseas. So some of the bicycles sold at Corliss Cycles are made overseas.

Most of the novels on this year's prize shortlist were written by first-time authors. Some first-time authors have received writing grants. So some novels on the shortlist were written by authors who received writing grants.

Some restaurants that passed last month's health inspection got a reminder notice from the city. After all, most restaurants that passed were also inspected the year before, and every restaurant inspected the year before got one.

Every greenhouse at the Ames nursery is heated entirely by solar panels. No greenhouse that is heated entirely by solar panels needs a backup generator. So none of the greenhouses at the Ames nursery needs a backup generator.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: most A are B, every B is C, so some A are C. D has exactly this form once it is rearranged: it gives its conclusion first, then 'most that passed were inspected the year before' and 'every restaurant inspected the year before got a notice.' A is the trap: it matches the original's order and also concludes 'some,' but its second premise says 'most' rather than 'every,' and two 'most' statements need not overlap, so it is invalid. B and C are likewise invalid, and E is valid but has a different, all-and-none form.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some paintings cleaned with the new solvent were approved for loan.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most cleaned paintings showed no varnish clouding; every painting with no clouding was approved for loan.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; all B are C; so some A are C (valid).

breakdown.analysis: Is it valid? Yes. The A's that are B (most of them) are all C, because every B is C, so at least some A's are C. We need another valid "most + every → some" argument. Most students pick (A) because it reads in the same order and ends with the same "some." But its second link is "most," not "every." Two "mosts" can miss each other: the orchestra's conservatory graduates could be the ones who can't sight-read. The right answer, (D), states its conclusion first and its premises after "After all." Rearrange before you match.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Same order, same "some" conclusion. But "most" in the second premise breaks it: the orchestra's conservatory graduates could all be in the minority who can't sight-read. Invalid, so not parallel to a valid argument.
Every A is B; most B are C; so some A are C. Invalid: the Corliss bikes could all be among the warranty bikes made at home.
"Some first-time authors" got grants, but they need not be the shortlisted ones. Invalid.
CORRECT. Rearranged: most that passed were inspected the year before; every one inspected the year before got a notice; so some that passed got a notice. Most A are B, all B are C, so some A are C.
Valid, but a different shape: all A are B, no B is C, so no A is C. No "most," no "some."
